#4507. Smart home gift guide: 40 clever gadgets to make any living space better using automation

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 9:45 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

The best smart home gift is the one that works the day it’s unwrapped, without a ladder, a landlord’s sign-off, or a surprise subscription. This guide covers every type of smart home dweller, from beginner to full-on Tony Stark. We started with easy plug-and-play options like a four-pack of Kasa Matter smart plugs and Philips Hue Essential bulbs that get up and running in minutes, along with new 2026 hardware we’ve tested hands-on, like Apple’s HomeView display. At the other end, upgrades like the Nest Learning Thermostat and the Emporia Vue 3 energy monitor reward a little more installation work.

Before you buy, find out which smart home platform your recipient already uses. Alexa, Google Home, and Apple Home still don’t share everything, though Matter-certified gear like the Eve Energy plug and the Govee Floor Lamp 2 works with all three. Some Matter devices connect over Thread, a low-power wireless network that needs a hub called a border router, such as a HomePod mini 2 or a Google TV Streamer, to reach the rest of the house. The entries flag the hubs, extra hardware, and monthly plans that can turn a gift into homework. Prices come from makers and major retailers and were checked in November 2026, so expect them to move during holiday sales.

If you’re shopping for a cook, the smart ovens and smokers are in our kitchen gift guide. If you’re building out a whole system rather than shopping for one gift, start with our guide to the best smart home devices.

Amazon kept the old shape and changed the guts inside. The sixth-generation Echo Dot adds a built-in smart home hub for Zigbee, Matter, and Thread gear, so it can pair devices on its own instead of leaning on a separate bridge. Amazon also claims 50 percent more bass than the model it replaces, though anyone buying primarily for music should watch for holiday discounts or spend $20 more on the Echo Dot Max. Its built-in eero extender stretches Wi-Fi by up to 1,000 square feet in houses that already run eero, and Alexa+ is included with Prime or costs $19.99 a month without it.

An all-in-one gift for backyard birdwatchers, the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro pairs 4K HDR with PDAF Auto Focus for sharp close-ups, plus 1080p/120 fps slow motion for fleeting moments. FeatherPal AI identifies more than 10,000 species with an eligible subscription, while the 5W solar roof and removable hopper simplify upkeep. Now $199.99—save $60 at its lowest price of the year through December 27.

Google went six years without a new smart speaker before the Google Home Speaker arrived in June. Built around Gemini for Home, it includes a Thread border router and handles everyday jobs like switching lights and adjusting a thermostat without a subscription. Gemini Live conversations and extra AI features require Google Home Premium, which starts at $10 a month. Buy it for someone who already runs their house from the Google Home app.

The hub that makes Apple Home work away from home

For a household built around iPhones, the HomePod mini 2 is the speaker that lets Apple’s Home app run automations and control gear from away. It runs on an S10 chip with Wi-Fi 6E and Thread, acting as a hub for HomeKit and Matter accessories. Buy it for that hub job first: Apple says Siri’s bigger AI upgrades arrive in a future software update, and the personal features need an iPhone or iPad that supports Apple Intelligence. An Apple TV 4K handles the same hub duties for anyone who would rather have a streaming box.

Apple’s first smart display doubles as a home hub

Apple’s first smart display, HomeView, puts a 7-inch touchscreen on the kitchen counter for music, FaceTime calls, and Apple Home controls, while serving as a home hub alongside the HomePod mini 2. In our hands-on review, we found it very helpful, if a little quirky.

It recognizes up to six people by face and surfaces their own messages, calendars, and reminders, though only when that person’s paired iPhone or iPad is nearby and recently unlocked. Stick to the tabletop model as a gift: the wall-mounted version starts at the same $299, but it requires a separate Schneider Home wall mount starting at $59.95 (plus a user-supplied 20-watt USB-C power adapter for the base mount).

Philips Hue used to be the smart bulb you bought only after getting serious about smart home tech. The Hue Essential line changes the math with an affordable four-pack of color bulbs that connect over Bluetooth and work from the Hue app without a bridge. Each bulb puts out 800 lumens and dims down to 2 percent. Adding them to Alexa, Google Home, or Apple Home runs through Matter and takes a compatible hub, such as an Echo, a Nest Hub, or a HomePod mini 2, and they can always move onto a Hue Bridge later.

Two color bulbs that work with every major platform

A pair of GE Cync Full Color bulbs is a low-stakes way to test smart lighting on two bedside lamps. They connect straight to 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi in the Cync app with no hub, and Matter support brings them into Alexa, Google Home, Apple Home, and SmartThings when paired with a compatible Matter hub. Each puts out 800 lumens, matching the Hue Essential bulbs above, and if the recipient hates smart home gear, they still work like regular bulbs.

Four plugs that work with every major assistant

This four-pack of Kasa Matter smart plugs is the easiest way to automate something your recipient already owns, whether that’s a lamp, a holiday tree, or a coffee maker. Each slim plug leaves the second wall outlet free, handles up to 15 amps, tracks energy use, and connects to Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Home through Matter. Just note that they only join a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network.

Buy Eve Energy for someone who doesn’t want a living-room lamp checking in with a company server. Eve says it needs no cloud account or registration, and it communicates locally over Matter and Thread while tracking power draw. Because it relies on Thread, the house needs a border router like a HomePod mini 2 or a Google TV Streamer. At $39.95, you’re paying nearly as much for one plug as you would for the Kasa four-pack above.

The GE Cync Outdoor Smart Plug puts holiday lights and porch string lights on two independently controlled outlets rated for wet locations, with covers for both sockets and a 15-amp ceiling. This model connects to Alexa and Google Assistant straight over Wi-Fi. Its Amazon listing doesn’t mention Apple Home, so iPhone households should look for GE’s newer Matter-compatible version instead.

Four outlets that work with Apple Home too

Competition for outlets is fierce behind my desk and TV. It’s probably like that for you, too. The Meross Smart Power Strip has four outlets that switch independently, so the TV, the game console and the lamp behind them can each follow a different schedule. Its four USB ports switch as a group, and surge protection is built in. It connects over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi with no hub and works with Apple Home, Alexa, Google Home and SmartThings, though controlling it through Apple Home from outside the house takes a home hub like a HomePod mini 2.

Color accent lighting for Apple, Google and Alexa homes

Despite what an electrician will tell you, it’s possible to revamp a room’s lighting without breaking into the wiring. The Govee Floor Lamp 2 is rated for up to 1,725 lumens, with independent lighting for the pole and base. Matter support drops it straight into Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, or SmartThings without a Govee-only workaround, though it ships in pieces, so plan on a few minutes of assembly.

Christmas lights that know the shape of the tree

Unlike standard app-controlled holiday lights that just change color, Twinkly Strings use a phone’s camera to map where every bulb sits on the tree, then animate patterns across that exact shape. This 100-LED Gen II strand connects over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth and can’t be cut to length. Twinkly says you can sync up to 4,000 LEDs across multiple sets, which helps, since 100 bulbs won’t cover a full-size tree on their own.

Give the Hatch Restore 3 to anyone who dreads a phone alarm blaring six inches from their face. It brightens gradually like a sunrise in the morning and handles wind-down lighting and sound at night. Sunrise alarms, wind-down lights, and a basic sound library all work without a subscription, while the optional Hatch+ sleep library runs $5.99 a month or $59.99 a year after a 30-day free trial.

Family members add photos and videos to the Aura Carver from Aura’s app, so new pictures keep showing up long after the holidays, with no subscription and no storage limit. The 10.1-inch landscape screen pairs two portrait shots side by side so they fill the display. You can preload photos before it ships so it comes out of the box ready to go. Just double-check which album you pick before Grandma gets an unexpected slideshow.

Sized for a bedroom, controlled from a phone

This gift doesn’t have to be passive-aggressive, but it can be. Levoit recommends the Core 300S-P for bedrooms and offices up to 219 square feet, since the 1,058-square-foot figure in its listings assumes only one air change an hour. It connects to the free VeSync app for remote control, responds to Alexa and Google Assistant, and ships with a three-stage filter already installed alongside an indicator that flags when it needs replacing.

Answers the question of whether the cat ate

The Petlibro Granary Smart Camera Feeder answers the question every pet owner texts the sitter: Did the cat eat? It holds 5 liters of kibble, connects over 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz Wi-Fi, and schedules dry-food meals from an app while watching the bowl with a 1080p, 145-degree night-vision camera and two-way audio. Petlibro’s Video Cloud plans start at $59.99 a year for seven days of storage, or clips can be saved locally to a microSD card (sold separately).

Think of the Google TV Streamer as an entertaining Trojan horse for sneaking a smart hub into the living room. Beyond 4K HDR with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, it doubles as a Matter hub and Thread border router, anchoring gear like the Eve Energy plug and putting a home control panel right on the TV. Google doesn’t include an HDMI cable, so tuck one into the gift bag.

Person and pet alerts without a monthly bill

Unwrapping a gadget that immediately hands you a monthly bill is a terrible gift experience, which is why the Tapo C120 keeps its subscription optional. It distinguishes people, pets, and vehicles without a paid plan and saves footage to a microSD card up to 512 GB (not included). You get 2K QHD video, color night vision from dual spotlights, Alexa and Google Assistant support, and an IP66 rating for outdoor use wherever an outlet is in reach of its power cord. Tapo Care cloud storage is there only if you want it.

For a front door without existing wiring, the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K (2nd gen) runs on a built-in rechargeable battery and records Retinal 2K video with 6× zoom. Ring’s $49.99 Solar Charger keeps it topped up for anyone who doesn’t want to pull it off the frame to recharge. Saving and reviewing clips does require a Ring subscription, with Ring Solo covering one device for $4.99 a month.

A smart lock that keeps the landlord’s key working

Because the SwitchBot Lock Ultra mounts over the inside thumbturn of an existing deadbolt, renters get smart access without replacing the cylinder or cutting off the landlord’s key.

This Vision Combo bundles a keypad that unlocks with 3D facial recognition alongside a Hub Mini for remote control and Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Home support. Some deadbolt shapes need a separate $20 adapter kit, so take a quick look at the door before you wrap it.

Sticking a SwitchBot Bot next to a coffee maker or air conditioner gives an old appliance a tiny robotic finger to push its button on command. It sticks next to a rocker switch or push button with an adhesive pad. Out of the box, it runs over Bluetooth in the SwitchBot app; remote access and voice commands through Alexa, Google Assistant, or Siri require a separate SwitchBot hub.

The battery-powered Hue Dimmer Switch puts a real button back on the wall for houseguests, mounting with adhesive or screws and lifting off its magnetic plate to work from the couch. It dims Hue lights and cycles through scenes, and Hue’s setup guide says it can pair directly with up to 10 bulbs. App customization and routines still require a Hue Bridge, so it makes the most sense for someone who already owns one.

Stick the Aqara Door and Window Sensor P2 on a door or window, and opening it can switch on a hall light or fire off a phone alert. It runs on a CR123A battery and joins Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, or SmartThings over Matter and Thread. Make sure the recipient already has a Thread border router like the HomePod mini 2 or Google TV Streamer, because the sensor won’t work without one.

Three sensors for the spots that flood first

A leak sensor may seem like a boring gift until you consider the pain of a water heater disaster. This GoveeLife Water Leak Detector 1s kit bundles three IP67-rated sensors and a Wi-Fi gateway that sends a phone alert when one of them gets wet, while each puck sounds a 105-decibel alarm. Govee claims five years of battery life. Tuck them under the water heater, the washing machine, and the kitchen sink.

The Rachio Smart Hose Timer threads onto an outdoor faucet, runs schedules from Rachio’s app, and skips a watering when rain is in the forecast. The starter kit includes one valve and the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi hub it requires, and a single hub can manage up to eight valves. Grab a pair of AA batteries (not included), and in cold climates remind the recipient it’s a gift for spring that needs to come indoors before a hard freeze.

Solar power, two lenses and no monthly bill

Mounted outdoor cameras are a pain to pull down for charging, so the eufy SoloCam S340 brings its own solar panel, which eufy says stays topped up on two hours of direct sun a day. It pairs a 3K wide-angle lens and a 2K telephoto lens for 8× hybrid zoom, pans 344 degrees, saves clips to 8 GB of built-in storage with no monthly fee, and works with Alexa and Google Assistant. At full MSRP, it sits just $10 under eufy’s newer SoloCam E50 ($229.99), so watch for holiday discounts on the S340 or check which model the listing shows.

The alarm Google sells now that the Nest Protect is gone

Google stopped making the Nest Protect, and the First Alert SC5 is the smart alarm the Google Store sells in its place. It detects smoke and carbon monoxide, sends phone alerts, and can be checked, silenced, or tested from the First Alert or Google Home apps. It even interconnects with existing Nest Protects so every unit sounds together, making it a timely drop-in swap as older Nest Protects reach their expiration dates after about 10 years. This battery model needs no wiring, though homes with hardwired alarms should opt for First Alert’s hardwired version instead.

Comes with a sensor for the room that’s always too hot

Our utility bills went haywire last year, and that makes the math on a smart thermostat much more attractive. Google’s fourth-generation Nest Learning Thermostat includes a Nest Temperature Sensor for the room that never feels right, is designed to work in most homes without a common power wire (C-wire), and supports Matter so it also shows up in Apple Home. It’s sold only in the U.S. and Canada.

The ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium packs a lot onto one wall plate: radar occupancy detection, an indoor air quality monitor, and a built-in Alexa speaker, plus a remote SmartSensor in the box. Siri works on it too in homes that already have a HomePod or HomePod mini 2. The company claims it can cut heating and cooling costs by up to 26 percent, or as much as $284 a year, and fit more than 95 percent of HVAC systems.

Unlocks with a tap of an iPhone or Apple Watch

The Schlage Encode Plus is the deadbolt to buy for iPhone households, unlocking with a tap of an iPhone or Apple Watch via Apple Home Keys while also supporting Alexa and Google Assistant. Built-in Wi-Fi means no separate bridge for the Schlage app, Alexa, or Google, though remote Apple Home control takes a home hub like a HomePod mini 2 or Apple TV.

Schlage’s app manages up to 100 access codes for guests and dog walkers, and a physical backup key comes in the box. Schlage estimates four AA batteries last up to six months with typical use. Because it replaces the whole deadbolt, confirm the recipient is allowed to swap theirs before wrapping it.

Smart lights that survive someone flipping the switch

Put the Lutron Diva smart dimmer on your list for anyone tired of guests killing smart bulbs at the wall. It replaces the switch with a familiar paddle, and this starter kit bundles Lutron’s Caséta hub and a Pico remote to tie the lights into Alexa, Apple Home, Google Home, Ring, and Sonos. Better yet, it handles up to 150 watts of LEDs without needing a neutral wire (the extra return wire missing from many older switch boxes).

The Meross MSG100HK puts an end to circling back down the street to check whether the garage door closed. It wires into an existing opener instead of replacing the motor, requires no subscription, and covers Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Assistant. Run the opener through Meross’s compatibility checker first, since Chamberlain, LiftMaster, and Craftsman units may need a separate accessory that Meross ships at no charge.

Skips the watering when it already rained

Rachio has sold the Rachio 3 for years, and it’s still the company’s main sprinkler controller. It replaces the timer on an existing in-ground irrigation system, installs in 30 minutes or less according to Rachio, and runs on a free app with weather skips that hold off on watering after rain. A 16-zone version costs $249.99, and the controller pairs with the Tempest weather station further down this list.

Find out which circuit is eating the electric bill

The Emporia Vue 3 shows which circuits are eating the electric bill, though it can’t separate two appliances that share a circuit. The kit includes two main sensors and 16 branch sensors, and the company claims customers save an average of 10 percent on their bills.

Those sensors clamp onto wires inside the breaker panel, so plan on an electrician unless the recipient is qualified to work in one.

For anyone who wonders what’s floating around their house, with or without a basement, the Airthings View Plus tracks odorless radon alongside fine dust (PM2.5), carbon dioxide, chemical fumes (VOCs), humidity, temperature, and air pressure with no subscription. Airthings says it runs up to two years on six AA batteries, or it can stay plugged in over USB-C.

The Eureka E20 Evo Plus docks at a bagless self-emptying station, so there are no replacement bags to reorder. It’s rated for 10,000 Pa of suction and maps rooms with lidar. Eureka says the station’s 2-liter bin needs emptying every couple of weeks in a typical home, though the trade-off is dumping that dusty bin into the trash by hand.

A backyard weather station with no moving parts

Turn a backyard into a personal weather lab with the Tempest Weather Station. It uses zero moving parts, measuring wind with ultrasonic sensors and rain with a haptic sensor, and feeds those readings into its own local forecasts with no subscription. The 2026 revision adds bigger solar panels and a replaceable battery.

It integrates with Alexa, Siri, IFTTT, and Rachio, so a rainy morning can cancel the sprinklers automatically. A flat base and pole mount come in the box, but supplying the actual fence post or mast in an open spot is up to the buyer.

Turns existing Hue bulbs into motion sensors

Anyone with a pile of Hue bulbs will get more out of a Hue Bridge Pro than another lamp. It supports more than 150 lights, and Philips says it responds five times faster than the standard bridge. Its MotionAware feature turns groups of three or four compatible Hue bulbs into motion sensors that switch lights on automatically, though security motion alerts and alarms require a paid plan.

One interface for a house full of gadgets

For the person who already owns half of this list, the next gift is a single interface to wrangle it all. Home Assistant Green arrives with the open-source Home Assistant software preinstalled, plugs into a router over Ethernet, and packs 4 GB of RAM and 32 GB of storage. Zigbee gear requires a separate Home Assistant Connect ZBT-2 adapter.

The software is free and runs locally inside the house. Reaching it remotely, or linking it to Alexa or Google Assistant, takes either networking know-how or Nabu Casa’s optional Home Assistant Link subscription ($6.50 a month or $65 a year). Nabu Casa raised the box’s suggested price to $199 this year, citing memory costs.

#4503. The pumpkin’s strange journey from toxic plant to a seasonal staple

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 10:20 AM EST

From jack-o-lanterns and cute tabletop knickknacks to pumpkin pie and the ever popular pumpkin spice latte, the iconic squash fills every nook and cranny of the fall season. But the vegetable has taken a long and strange journey to become our favorite autumnal symbol.

Logan Kistler, an anthropologist at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, is interested in the origin stories of the crops that feed humanity. And squashes have a strange one. They evolved in the Americas before corn and beans, and played an important role in the start of agriculture in the two continents, he tells Popular Science.

It’s worth highlighting that pumpkins are a type of squash. Indeed, “pumpkin” is not an official botanical term, Kistler points out. Squashes, along with zucchini and some gourds, belong to the genus Cucurbita, which is within the broader family Cucurbitaceae, which includes melons, watermelons, cucumbers, and other kinds of gourds.

“Out of this genus Cucurbita at least six different independent lineages of squashes, pumpkins, gourds, and things like that evolved in several different places in the Americas, more or less simultaneously,” says Kistler. However, “the quirky thing about this genus and about a lot of members of this family is in the wild they are unpalatably nasty. They’re incredibly bitter.”

That bitterness comes from high concentrations of cucurbitacins. The compounds are the most bitter natural substances that scientists know of. Humans can’t stomach that level of bitterness, but paleontologists have discovered that mastodons (extinct elephant-like mammals) were eating them 30,000 years ago. And that means disseminating them through their feces.

Today, there is no such megafauna in North America that can withstand wild squashes—they’ve lost their evolutionary partner. Cue humans, whose landscaping-shaping settlements give Cucurbita a new ecological niche to fit into.

“You can kind of think of it as, they lose their one mutualistic partner and then they can just kind of cozy up into this new disturbed landscape that’s created by humans. But then for that relationship to make any sense, they can’t be unpalatably bitter and they can’t be toxic,” Kistler explains.

It appears that these wild squashes had to make, “that evolutionary concession to soften the rind, become less toxic, more palatable and reap the benefits of the protection and care of human cultivators.”

It seems to have worked. The genus spread far and wide, and wherever it overlaps with humans, they are making use of it. For example, the pumpkins we use to make jack-o-lanterns every Halloween originated in Mexico approximately 10,000 years ago, and there is evidence of humans domesticating them there very early on.

Ultimately, the transition from extremely bitter mastodon snack to today’s autumnal epitome probably involved both Cucurbita’s natural evolutionary journey as well as human intervention. “I tend to think about domestication as, at least in the early phases, the plant is adapting to life alongside humans and that has benefits to humans,” says Kistler, adding that at some point people will get involved more directly.

But it doesn’t seem like many of these earliest domestication efforts were carried out with the goal of food production. In Florida, they may have been used as fishnet floats, and in the southwestern United States they were likely put to use as containers.

They were eventually carved and—as we all know—baked into pies.

Ready to trade your controller for a steering wheel? This Logitech setup is a great place to start, especially at this price.

#4499. NASA spacecraft created stadium-sized crater after slamming into asteroid

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 12:30 PM EST

After over four years of years of anticipation, the European Space Agency has obtained images detailing the aftermath of NASA’s head-on collision with the asteroid Dimorphos. The photos and scans from ESA’s Hera spacecraft highlight the results of the Double Asteroid Redirection Test’s (DART) intentional run-in with Didymos’ 500-foot-wide moonlet Dimorphos in 2022, revealing a stadium-sized crater, cloud of boulders, and a new, erratic orbital path.

“Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same,” Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement. “Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once!”

Michel explained that while DART flattened one side of Dimorphos into a massive crater, the rest of the space rock isn’t much different. Fields of boulders largely remain where they could be seen in DART’s photos from 2022, although the event did drastically change the binary system’s surroundings.

“Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size,” added mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

Hera employed three instruments during its first observations—a thermal infrared imager to measure surface temperature, a 25-color multispectral imager, and a monochrome camera.

The car-sized probe’s work is only just getting started, too. In December, Hera will ultimately travel to barely eight miles from the asteroids, while obtaining increasingly higher-resolution photos. The spacecraft will then deploy a pair of CubeSats to get even closer to the binary system in January 2027. If all goes as planned, one of those devices will even attempt to land on the surface of Dimorphos. The combined measurements from this phase will help researchers understand the impact’s efficiency and improve future deflection strategies.

Hera’s first images were debuted at the dinosaur hall of the Berlin Natural History Museum—an intentional choice on the team’s part.

“Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid impact changed the course of life on Earth,” said Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. “Today, for the first time in history, humanity is validating how to prevent such an event from happening again.”

#4496. Three-flippered sea turtle named Endor healing in California

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 1:00 PM EST

In July, a green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) found itself in a bind. Like many unlucky marine and aquatic animals, this turtle ended up tangled in fishing line. But this reptile’s luck was about to change. Volunteers with the Aquarium of the Pacific’s Southern California Sea Turtle Monitoring community science program were out gathering field data on the green sea turtles spotted in the San Gabriel River in Santa Barbra, California.

The first attempt at a rescue was unsuccessful. The sea turtle was swimming in deep water with low visibility, so it could not be reached. But by the next day, the team saw the turtle swimming in an area of the river easier to access.

The roughly 70-pound turtle is now receiving behind-the-scenes care at the Aquarium of the Pacific. According to the aquarium, the fishing line caused a severe constriction injury on its the sea turtle’s left flipper. The reptile also swallowed some of the fishing line, risking damage to its internal organs.

“When the sea turtle came to us, it had a fishing line constriction that caused severe damage to its flipper,” Aquarium of the Pacific veterinarian Dr. Brittany Stevens said in an emailed statement. “Despite all efforts over the past few months, unfortunately, the left flipper could not be saved and had to be amputated to aid in the turtle’s recovery.”

This is not the aquarium’s first experience with three-flippered turtles. The team rescued and rehabilitated a green sea turtle named Porkchop, who was released into the wild in February. Porkchop has since been spotted by aquarium volunteers who monitor sea turtles.

The turtle now named Endor is receiving wound care and antibiotics as it goes through rehabilitation, with the goal of eventually returning to the wild. Endor is a sub-adult, meaning it is past the juvenile stage, and approaching sexual maturity, but not yet a full adult turtle. The sex has not been determined and Endor was previously tagged by NOAA in 2025.

As Endor is rehabilitated, it will eventually move from the behind-the-scenes sea turtle care area to a rehabilitation area open for public viewing. Meatloaf, an over 250-pound rescued green sea turtle, is currently living in that space.

The Aquarium of the Pacific has been caring for several turtle species since 2000, including green, olive ridley (Lepidochelys olivacea), and loggerhead (Caretta caretta). All sea turtle species found in U.S. waters are listed as endangered or threatened and are protected by the Endangered Species Act.

To find a licensed animal rescue and rehabilitation organization in your area, visit Animal Help Now or call your local animal control department.

#4494. Two-Thirds of Dementia Content On TikTok Is Misleading, Researchers Say

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new survey suggests that about two-thirds of dementia advice videos on TikTok are misleading

Of the videos examined, the analysis shows that nearly half contained inaccurate and potentially damaging information.

The researchers say that approximately 44% of TikTok creators who share dementia content lack credibility and appropriate qualifications.

Although misleading dementia content may appear on other social media platforms, this research examined only TikTok content, warranting further investigation.

The survey was commissioned by Homewatch Caregivers and has not been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

A spokesperson for TikTok told Healthline that if health-related content is potentially harmful, it is flagged for removal. The spokesperson added that 99.6% of misinformation deemed violative was proactively removed from the platform in 2026.

The spokesperson added that TikTok relies on fact-checking and guidance from public health authorities to help assess the accuracy of content. The platform may also apply warning labels to content that cannot be verified as accurate.

Looking to social media for health information is not uncommon. A recent poll reports that 31% of adults in the United States use social media at least once a month to look for health information and advice.

Experts advise seeking information about dementia from trusted sources, such as a primary care doctor and organizations like the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and the Alzheimer’s Association, rather than social media, where content creators who share advice often lack expertise.

“It’s normal to want answers quickly when you’re caring for someone living with dementia, and a short video from someone who seems to know what they’re talking about can be really convincing,” said lead researcher Jennifer Winarski, senior manager of care operations and quality for Homewatch CareGivers.

“Despite there being some genuinely helpful information out there, you don’t always know whether it’s backed by medical evidence, so we wanted to bring our own expertise to uncover whether popular TikToks can be trusted,” she told Healthline. “We hope our report will encourage people to be a bit more careful about what they act on.”

For the survey, researchers selected a sample of 500 of the most-watched dementia-related videos on TikTok with hashtags such as:

Researchers then transcribed the video data to assess its accuracy.

The researchers found that two-thirds (66.4%) of the popular TikTok videos contained misleading information. Of those videos, about half (47.6%) contained potentially damaging misleading dementia information.

“It’s clear that many of the creators mean well, but much of what we saw was personal opinion rather than proven information, and in a few cases, general good health tips were presented as if they were specifically helpful for individuals living with dementia,” Winarski said.

“If families act on that, they could end up spending time and money on things that won’t help — and in the worst of cases, it could delay getting the support their loved one really needs,” she added.

Dung Trinh, MD, an internist for MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of the Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, said it’s important to be aware of the volume of misleading dementia information on social media. Trinh was not involved in this survey.

Some people may be making decisions about their health based on incomplete, misleading, or incorrect information, he said.

“For example, someone might see a video claiming that a particular supplement can reverse Alzheimer’s disease or that certain memory problems automatically mean someone has dementia,” Trinh said.

“These messages can lead to unnecessary fear, false reassurance, wasted money, or delays in getting a proper diagnosis.”

“We are entering an exciting era in Alzheimer’s care, with advances in blood-based biomarkers, earlier detection, and treatments that may slow disease progression in appropriately selected patients,” Trinh continued.

“Getting an accurate diagnosis and receiving timely medical guidance are becoming increasingly important.”

The researchers examined the content creators behind the TikTok videos included in their analysis. They found that 44% of video creators behind the misleading videos had no relevant qualifications.

Rehan Aziz, MD, vice chair of education in the Department of Psychiatry at Hackensack Meridian Jersey Shore University Medical Center and associate professor of psychiatry and neurology at the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine in New Jersey, said that content creators offering dementia advice should have relevant qualifications. Aziz wasn’t involved in the survey.

“Start by looking at the creator’s profile for a full name and a specific credential, such as MD, DO, PhD, or RN, along with a specialty,” Aziz told Healthline.

“For dementia, the most relevant experts include neurologists, geriatric psychiatrists, geriatricians, neuropsychologists, and nurses, including advanced practice nurses, or social workers who specialize in dementia care.”

“You can confirm a doctor’s license through your state’s licensing board website and check board certification at certificationmatters.org,” Aziz said.

As of 2020, more than 55 million people worldwide were living with dementia — a neurological condition that negatively affects the brain. Researchers predict this number will hit 78 million by 2030.

The increase in the number of people seeking dementia content online is a reflection of this trend.

When looking for accurate dementia information and guidance, Nestor Beltre, MD, a neurologist with Baptist Health Kenneth C. Griffin Neuroscience Institute, part of Baptist Health South Florida, said a great first step is to speak with their primary care physician. Beltre wasn’t involved in the survey.

“Memory changes can occur for many different reasons, and some causes, including vitamin deficiencies, depression, and certain medical conditions, may be treatable,” he told Healthline.

“Early evaluation can help identify what may be contributing to these changes and determine the most appropriate next steps. Depending on the individual’s symptoms, a neurologist, psychiatrist, or neuropsychologist can provide further evaluation and guidance,” Belter continued.

Beltre advised turning to trusted resources such as the Alzheimer’s Association and the National Institute on Aging, which can increase public understanding of memory-related conditions and available treatment options.

“The most important message is that patients and families have resources available to help them better understand and manage cognitive health,” he said.

#4492. Adorable black bear sleeps with his head on his paw

Published Nov 25, 2026 1:52 PM EST

We’ve all watched dogs or cats twitch their ears and paws as they contentedly sleep away the day. And it turns out that black bears (Ursus americanus) have adorable sleeptime spasms, too—as one small black bear named ‘Nugget’ demonstrated in a video captured at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska.

In honor of his endearing, jerk-filled sleep, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded Nugget the Biggest Dreamer Award. Nugget was seen peacefully snoozing on a rock with his head resting on one of his giant paws as flies flit around his face.

“With ears and nose twitching away, Nugget was off in what seemed to be a very pleasant dreamland,” the rangers write. “Does watching make you wonder what he’s dreaming about? It must be salmon, right?”

The rangers have already awarded Nugget two other awards this year, including the Annoying Sibling Award and the Introvert Award. He may just receive the most awards of any Anan Creek bear in the forest! Go Nugget!

Nugget is easy to spot among the bears who frequent the salmon-filled Anan Creek. He’s a bit smaller and has fur that changes from a tufty red in spring to sleek black coat in autumn. His unique coloring also makes it look like he has goggles around his eyes. Rangers named him Nugget in 2024, and he’s been seen at Anan Creek ever since.

As Nugget snoozed alongside the burbling water, other black and brown bears came and went as they had their fill of salmon. As the rangers write, his tranquil sleep among the other bears is “a testament to the amazing ecosystem at Anan Wildlife Observatory.”

Despite his three awards, Nugget is far the only bear (or mink!) getting awards this season. Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the dozens of bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska this past summer.

The largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and—of course—plenty of bears.

One of the bear hotspots in the forest is Anan Creek. The creek has one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska, making it a popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their more portly counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast at the creek and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear at Anan Creek has their own behaviors and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior. Tune in next year to decide who ought to win the Biggest Dreamer award next!

#4488. Dark energy camera captures ethereal Betta Fish Nebula

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Ghostly blue clouds about 6,800 light-years from Earth are all that remain of an ancient cosmic demise. These and other details are visible in the most recent look at a supernova remnant classified as SNR G295.5+09.7. Depending on how you see it, SNR G295.5+09.7 likely earns at least one of its nicknames: the Betta Fish or Mermaid Nebula.

A supernova remnant encompasses vast swirling waves of dust, gas, and stellar material created in the wake of a star’s death. SNR G295.5+09.7 exploded between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago in the Centaurus constellation, ejecting its outer layers of matter to collide with interstellar space’s own gases. The energy from these interactions subsequently caused the region to glow, which is now detectable by highly sensitive instruments. In this case, astronomers imaged the Betta Fish nebula using the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera (DECam) located at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile.

Although impossible to see with the naked eye, the supernova remnant contains the last vestige of its prior life in the form of a neutron star. The incredibly, miniscule dense object is what’s left from a star that was once multiple times the mass as our sun. Even now, SNR G295.5+09.7’s neutron star is larger than the solar system’s anchor—cramming about 1.4 times the sun’s into a sphere barely 12-miles in diameter. As the National Science Foundation’s National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory noted in its announcement, the stellar object is so small that it could fit inside the city of Tucson, Arizona.

However, the Betta Fish Nebula almost never happened. If the dynamics were slightly different, the massive stellar object’s collapse could have generated a black hole instead of a neutron star. If that were the case, the glowing swirls of cosmic material would likely never escape the black hole’s unfathomable gravitational pull.

GLP-1 medications have transformed obesity and type 2 diabetes treatment. Now, researchers are investigating whether the effects of this blockbuster class of drugs extend beyond weight loss and affect brain health.

A comprehensive new review published on November 5 in the journal Science evaluated the current evidence on how GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide may affect the brain across aging, cardiometabolic disease, and Alzheimer’s disease.

The authors of the review suggested that GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Zepbound may offer brain health benefits. However, they were also left with the question of whether the medications act directly on the brain or whether better brain health is actually a consequence of improved cardiometabolic health.

Sheena Aurora, MD, vice president, Medical Affairs, Alzheimer’s Association, who wasn’t involved in the review, told Healthline that more research is needed to better understand the effects of GLP-1 drugs on the brain.

“While research suggests GLP-1s could reduce brain inflammation, improve blood vessel health, and even protect neurons, much broader, randomized clinical trials on GLP-1s and brain health, including in people with Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, are needed,” she said.

GLP-1 medications like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, mimic the GLP-1 hormone. Tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro and Zepbound, also targets a second hormone pathway called GIP.

These medications have been shown to produce significant weight loss and improvements in cardiometabolic health.

This is important for brain health because obesity, type 2 diabetes, and vascular dysfunction are all linked with cognitive impairment and dementia. Insulin resistance and chronic inflammation may also link metabolic and brain health.

Analyses of large outcome trials and observational cohorts have suggested that GLP-1 medications may be associated with a reduced risk of cognitive impairment and dementia. However, randomized trials in diseases like Alzheimer’s disease have yet to demonstrate clinical benefits.

Around 200 preclinical and mechanistic studies have shown benefits for learning, memory, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal resilience, though results are heterogeneous in design and direction, so a clear consensus on magnitude and mechanism remains lacking.

It is also unclear how well GLP-1 medications reach the brain. They appear to reach certain areas, such as the hypothalamus, brainstem, and circumventricular organs, more readily than regions protected by the blood-brain barrier.

The report authors noted that some studies have shown that GLP-1 receptor agonists may reduce the risk of cognitive impairment and dementia in people with type 2 diabetes. This may be due to cognitive issues being linked to factors such as blood sugar, blood pressure, vascular health, and sleep.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline, “These findings are interesting, but like many of the other benefits associated with GLP-1 medications, a direct causal relationship has not yet been proven.”

“Rather, the benefits appear to be more closely tied to the reduction in obesity and better control of diabetes,” he said.

Aurora noted that growing evidence supports the heart-brain connection.

She cited new findings from the Alzheimer’s Association’s landmark U.S. POINTER study presented at the Clinical Trials in Alzheimer’s Disease (CTAD) conference November 16–19 in Boston, MA.

The research showed that the structured lifestyle intervention program also improved heart health risk factors, such as:

“U.S. POINTER can change those risk factors within 24 months, and better heart health risk-factor control was linked with better cognition,” Aurora said. “We’re also interested to see whether adding a drug like a GLP-1 to a U.S. POINTER-style lifestyle program improves cognition in at-risk older adults more than the program alone.”

To find out, the Alzheimer’s Association is funding the Prevention of Risk for Cognitive Decline through Combined Therapy (PROTECT-Cog) global phase 3 clinical trial.

PROTECT-Cog is a first-of-its-kind trial designed to evaluate whether combining a proven multidomain lifestyle intervention with a metabolism-targeting drug, like a GLP-1, can further reduce the risk of cognitive decline, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia in at-risk older adults.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the review, told Healthline, “I often remind my patients that what’s good for the heart is generally good for the brain.”

“The brain depends on a healthy cardiovascular system to deliver a constant supply of oxygen, glucose, and other nutrients. Conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol can damage blood vessels, promote chronic inflammation, and increase the risk of stroke and vascular cognitive impairment,” he said.

“Over time, these changes can also contribute to the development or progression of dementia.”

Trinh added that while GLP-1 medications can improve several cardiometabolic risk factors, these improvements do not automatically translate into proven dementia prevention.

“Regular physical activity, a heart-healthy diet, adequate sleep, and management of cardiovascular risk factors remain essential strategies for maintaining brain health as we age,” he said.

When the report authors turned their attention to more stringent tests on semaglutide in people already living with early Alzheimer’s disease, the picture began to change.

Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE + Phase 3 Trials examined the efficacy of semaglutide in people with early stage Alzheimer’s disease.

The studies showed that while semaglutide produced changes in several disease-related biomarkers, it didn’t slow the progression of Alzheimer’s disease.

This emphasizes that fixing metabolic issues might prevent cognitive decline in someone with obesity or diabetes. But it might not be enough to reverse the damage in someone with established Alzheimer’s disease, where profound synaptic loss and protein pathology have already occurred.

The review authors suggest that future research on obesity and diabetes should also include rigorous and specific cognitive testing.

#4486. New Zealand’s Twin-Engine Toyota Celica Is Essentially Unstoppable

A fairly conventional overlanding Celica build quickly spiraled into a monster with two engines, dual gearboxes, and semi-amphibious capability.

The art of modifying cars is gleefully rule-free. Sure, there are never-ending hoops to jump through for street legality, but actually building your perfect vehicle is merely a matter of dreams. For Kiwi Gareth Wadsworth, who goes by @garethcars on social media, those dreams meant stuffing two engines and two transmissions into a single sixth-generation Toyota Celica. Seems easy enough, right?

Wadsworth’s twin-engine Toyota Celica has made literal waves on social video in the past few weeks, as the Christchurch resident demonstrated its remarkable wading abilities in a series of viral videos. The basic recipe is a pair of Toyota’s 2.0-liter 3S-GE engines—one mounted in the front and one mounted in the rear—mated to a pair of manual transmissions and fed to individual differentials.

With so many moving parts, Wadsworth went analog with the controls; a pulley system attached to the original clutch pedal also operates the clutch for the rear transmission, and the throttle pedal is divided into an upper portion for the front engine and a lower portion for the rear engine. If you press directly in the middle of the accelerator, both engines will rev up (somewhat) in sync. Wadsworth emphasized that it is two completely separate drivetrains that require two of everything (two batteries, two fuel tanks, two ECUs, two radiators) and can be driven separately or simultaneously.

But this Celica build wasn’t always this extreme. In fact, the initial version was supposed to be a simple overlanding setup for a university off-road club trip in 2020. He initially off-roaded the Celica with a simple four-inch lift kit and 31-inch tires, but Wadsworth wanted to try something more extreme—and he didn’t want to abandon the existing platform.

“I had this Celica that I bought crashed, and I didn't have anything to do with it. I was a student. I didn't have the money for a four-wheel-drive, so I ended up building it into a four-wheel-drive,” Wadsworth said to Road & Track. “I paid $800 for the car, and then I sold the wheels and tires that were on it. So it was effectively a free car just sitting around, and I got some suspension left over from other projects that I threw in it, and the engine came from a crashed car I found upside down off the side of the road.”

After a year of mud-slinging fun, Wadsworth decided to go all-in on the dual-engine swap. The rear engine transplant only took two weeks, with most of the work happening after school and during a series of all-nighters. A day or two after the build was complete, Wadsworth and friends trailered the dual-engine Celica to an off-road area and began testing its abilities. Some limitations were quickly revealed.

“It was just the stock intakes for a few trips. It did have a snorkel on the outside for the front engine. Once it was twin-engine, it had enough power that we could hit the water faster, and that meant that the bow wave would keep going over the roof and filling the front engine's snorkel. We had one trip on the White Bear River that was in flood, and we hydrolocked the front engine twenty-three times, and we got sick of having to pull the spark plugs out, blasting the water out, and trying to get it running again. And so that's why I moved the intake to the glove box,” Wadsworth said.

Wading is one of the twin-engine Celica’s best tricks, as it is fast enough to glide onto the water and light enough to float through. The Celica has floated through currents that have sunk heavier 4x4 trucks, Wadsworth said. But the twin-engine Celica doesn’t just excel at water crossings, either. Because the gearboxes run independently, Wadsworth can tune the gear ratios of either end to suit his needs.

“There's no weird handling from the differences between the front and rear. It's just whichever engine's got the least load on it speeds up to catch up with the other one. They're effectively a fifty-fifty split,” Wadsworth said. “Because of the biasing, I quite often run almost exclusively rear-wheel-drive, and I only add front when I need it for traction. It's quite a unique feeling. It's so much fun, and probably the main reason I've still got it is being able to dynamically shift between front, rear, or four-wheel-drive and throttle biasing on the fly. In a mud pit, I can sit around doing donuts with the front in neutral, and then I can put the front-end gear in and let the clutch out slowly on the front to transition from donuts to power slides.”

And it isn’t even too hard to drive—relatively speaking. Wadsworth said that his mates can hop in and romp it with minimal coaching, at least in this configuration. Shifting the two gearboxes can get awkward, but the rear transmission shifter is placed near the traditional shifter, so you don’t have to reach far. Before the pulley clutch system, Wadsworth wired the rear clutch through the parking brake, which required a gentle touch to keep from stalling.

But it wasn’t always so accommodating. “On the original build, we didn't have time to connect any of the controls, so it had two drivers back then. And we didn't have a throttle, so the strap for tightening the hood was tied onto the rearview mirror and back to the rear throttle body, and you pulled it like a train horn,” Wadsworth said. “We certainly had a lot of difficulty driving it when we first built it, because it required two people to communicate—but it didn't have any exhaust, so we couldn't hear each other, and we had no total control on the rear; it was either fully on or fully off. And you had to get up out of your seat, turn around, and put it in gear for the rear engine.”

Even after six years of ownership and five years with two engines, Wadsworth plans to continue driving the twin-engine Celica as long as possible. Initially, he considered adding four-wheel steering using a power steering motor from a Nissan Leaf, but he said the time under the knife wouldn’t be worth it. The more time spent off-road, the better.

#4485. Toyota expands C-HR EV recall to 19,000 globally

Toyota is recalling 19,000 electric C-HR SUVs globally, with about 10,000 affected in the US.

In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.

Toyota initially said about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

According to Germany’s federal motor authority, Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the recall has now expanded to 19,000 C-HR vehicles globally. In Germany, the recall impacts 1,096 vehicles and is still under investigation by the KBA.

The issue stems from faulty software programming in the EV-ECU. While it’s intended to limit the battery’s charge level, the software can cause it to overcharge under certain conditions.

Toyota said the issue occurs if the battery is already at a high state of charge and the driver continues using the regenerative braking system.

When this happens, warning lights and a sound will alert the driver, and the electric drive system can shut down, causing the vehicle to lose power while driving.

Following an internal investigation, Toyota said in the NHTSA report that the issue was caused by incorrect software that disrupted the charging-limit function, allowing the battery to overcharge while driving.

The Toyota C-HR vehicles included in the recall were produced between June 17, 2025, and July 9, 2026.

In Europe and other overseas markets, Toyota sells the C-HR EV as the C-HR+ to distinguish it from the gas- or hybrid-powered version.

OTA would be great, but there are some systems that are isolated and can't be updated that way. The EV-ECU is a core function system that is very likely sealed to prevent tampering. They never expected to need to reprogram it. It's like the firmware on your phone.

Owners of affected vehicles in North America can take them to a Toyota dealership, where the battery ECU software will be updated free of charge.

Toyota mailed owner notification letters out on October 18, 2026. Owners can contact Toyota’s customer service at 1-800-331-4331. The recall number is 26TA17.

Other than saying the EV-ECU is being reprogrammed, Toyota has not yet announced next steps for owners of affected vehicles outside North America. The KBA reference number is 17116R.

Check back for more details. The recall only affects the 2026 C-HR. The 2027 Toyota C-HR is also now on sale.

#4484. 30+ editor-approved travel gifts for 2026

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Travel is the daily gift of life, but that doesn’t mean travel can’t suck the life out of you, even if you’re not going far. According to a study by the Institute of Environmental Science and Technology at the Autonomous University of Barcelona and McGill University, people travel an average of 78 minutes per day, regardless of mode of transport or distance covered. That means there’s a possibility of adventure in every bike ride, at each bus stop, and even while waiting in the airport security line. (You never know who will break liquid limits or forget to take their pepper spray off their keyring, giving everyone a delay and a story!) But you may also need accessories to keep the adventure comfortable.

No one knows that better than a friend or family member who is always heading to a new destination (typically very far, in this case). The best travel gifts bring more ease and peace of mind whether someone you know is dealing with 78 minutes’ worth of errands, cross-country travel, or long-haul international treks with a lifetime’s worth of layovers.

Other neck pillows don’t support neck movement in all directions; the Cabeau Evolution X Deluxe is a $70 neck pillow filled with customization to make it “just right,” just like Goldilocks. Change the pillow’s circumference, adjust the top or bottom lobes to change its height, and pull the adjustable cord and ball lock for a fine-tuned fit. Cooling vents release excess heat, and it comes with a travel case that compresses it down to half its size. This neck pillow is a 2026 Red Dot Design Awards winner for a reason.

It’s feather-light at 1 ounce, making it comfortable and lightweight. Contoured eye cups prevent pressure on the eyes and lashes, and the smooth-edged nose bridge prevents irritation. Plus, it’s designed to not pull or tangle your hair. It comes in seven color options, including lively options like butter yellow, lavender, and cornflower blue.

Going home for the holidays could mean pullout couches and cousins snoring. It could mean paper-thin hotel walls. It could mean poor sleep, unless you come prepared. Founded by three former Bose engineers, Ozlo makes earbuds for these eventualities. Each bud weighs only 1.6g and sits flush enough in the ear that they suit side sleepers no matter how bad the guest room pillow is. They don’t have active noise cancellation, but they do have soft silicone tips that passively block surroundings while adaptive masking sound covers the rest; a phone and Bluetooth aren’t even necessary. There’s even an accelerometer in them that registers when you nod off and switches off your podcast. A full charge lasts 14 hours, and a private in-ear alarm wakes only you, so you won’t disturb the whole house … or whoever shares your economy row. When dealing with the realities of travel and holiday hosting, Sleepbuds 2 are so much better than mere earplugs.

It’s hands-free, and they’re easier to shove into a backpack to meet the “carry-on and personal item” rule than a purse. My $25 JanSport Fifth Avenue Fanny Pack still holds up after years of heavy use. I’ll attach my keys to the strap, throw my favorite chapstick, headphones, and earplugs in the smaller front compartment, and stow my phone, wallet, and passport into the main compartment, which doesn’t eat my belongings like other purses in my possession. It’s served me well on daily commutes, errand runs, and neighborhood walks.

This carry-on is a splurge at $945, but its lifetime warranty and anodized aluminum shell mean it will last for many journeys, even after some rough-and-tumble handling from baggage people (that just adds personalized patina). It has TSA-compliant locks to stop snooping eyes and prevents the bag from bursting mid-flight. The 360-degree silent wheels let you drag or roll this luggage however you please. We also love this carry-on for its plentiful storage, including a zippered garment compartment and two internal pockets. A built-in compression pad with straps helps compact overpacking.

This $200 backpack from Thule is my go-to travel backpack and is my most-used personal item. The back panel fully unzips, letting me open the backpack fully like a suitcase. And I can rest easy knowing my electronics are protected in the plush 17-inch laptop and tablet sleeves. Its water-resistant finish keeps my wares dry in the rain, and the expandable middle section gives me more wiggle room when I’ve overpacked and lets me compress the goods when the bag is full.

Gear and Commerce Editor Tony Ware, meanwhile, is a huge fan of the 27L TuffSkin YETI Ranchero, which sports a Y-shaped easy-pull RipZip Opening in the front that provides full access to the pack’s main compartment and internal pockets, plus the GroundControl Base that ensures it stands upright when put down. This $395 piece of checked luggage from Monos is made from a durable, aerospace-grade polycarbonate shell, making it practically unbreakable and resistant to water and dents after hard impacts with walls, poles, and floors. The wraparound zipper adds almost two inches of depth, so you can pack an extra outfit or two (or bring back souvenirs). Handy features like a telescopic handle, whisper-quiet wheels, and a TSA-accepted lock allow for easy movin’ throughout the airport. Even the included freebies are practical: The roller luggage comes with an anti-microbial, silver ion-coated laundry bag, two shoe bags, and a vegan leather luggage tag.

The $219 40-Liter Baboon to the Moon Go-Bag is my duffel bag of choice for weekend trips or pet-sitting stints. Wherever she goes, I follow, thanks to a water-repellent coating, stash pockets, and—best of all—her agreeableness with TSA or gate agents as a carry-on. B2TM (the abbreviated name for the company) added a laptop sleeve and compression straps to its most recent version of the Go-Bag, meaning I can ditch my laptop backpack and pack smarter than ever, AKA: I can shove more crap in there. Not everyone likes big over-ear headphones (like the Bose above), or the feeling and more limited battery life of true wireless earbuds. Well, Marshall has a solution: The $229 on-ear Milton A.N.C. Bluetooth 6.0 headphones, which bring active noise cancellation to a less typical form factor. Six microphones feed the adaptive noise canceling, which is surprisingly effective despite not having the benefit of a complete seal around the ear. Plus, a charge lasts 50 hours with ANC on, and 15 minutes plugged in can get you 9.5 hours more, so New York to Singapore and back ain’t a thang. And adaptive loudness/EQ/spatial audio settings help give those days in the air even more vibes. There’s a USB-C-to-3.5mm cable for wired listening (just remember your seatback entertainment system adapter, and to have the headphones charged because they don’t run passively). They fold up and only weigh 200 grams, so they’re perfect in an already-stuffed personal item, maybe even a jacket pocket. And they’ve got that classic Marshall cool, all textured, leather-like vinyl with brass logo/control knobs. You’ll be rockin’ even when you’re not walkin’ …

We haven’t met wireless earbuds that haven’t announced “battery low” at some point before a flight ended, which isn’t optimal, especially if an attempt at getting some sleep is involved. But these $99 Bose wired earbuds will never give you up, never let you down, never get run down and desert you. Run off the USB-C port of any smartphone, tablet, or laptop, these bring back a newtro style Bose hasn’t made in a decade. And they are unlikely to discontinue it again anytime soon, considering the overwhelming positive response. Using the proprietary QuietControl algorithms that make other Sound By Bose products so good, they cut most perceived noise while providing a convenient three-button in-line remote that switches between Quiet, Aware, and off modes, plus offers playback controls. Plus, multiple eartip-and-stability band size combinations ensure a secure fit. And even if one comes loose on the way in/out of the included case, the 4.2-foot cable means you won’t have that moment of terror that an earbud rolled three rows back.

This $80 Anker Universal Charger combines compatibility with outlets from more than 200 countries into one power block charger. It detects local voltage in one second and is Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL)-certified for safe, stable charging. Unlike other international outlet adapters, this one is 25% smaller and designed to stay securely plugged in. And its USB-C/USB-A ports can charge four devices at once, including tech that requires higher voltage, like laptops and tablets.

No outlet is guaranteed in this world, but Anker’s $135 Laptop Power Bank keeps your devices charged when a place to plug in is nowhere to be found. Although it’s branded as a laptop power bank, it can also charge headphones, phones, handheld gaming devices, and more. It can charge an iPhone to full battery at least three times before running empty. The power hub can charge four devices at once. Two built-in USB-C cables mean you won’t have to root around for a charging cable when you need to recharge your tech. It also has a USB-A and USB-C port if you have a proprietary charger for a specific device.

Physical books can be clunky while traveling, especially as a voracious reader. The $160 Rakuten Kobo Clara is a black-and-white eReader that comes ad-free from the jump. I personally prefer it to the Amazon Kindle (which will cost you $170 to go ad-free) for this reason. The Rakuten Kobo Clara BW has 16 GB of storage and can carry up to 12,000 eBooks or 75 audiobooks. An optional Dark Mode makes for better nighttime or dark cabin reading, while ComfortLight PRO adjusts brightness, color temperature, and blue light to help you sleep easier while traveling.

This $80 JBL Clip 5 portable speaker packs pro sound into a pint-sized package. I always bring a small speaker like this one when I’m traveling so I can bump my getting-ready playlist from something that’s more powerful than my phone speakers. Pack it into a personal item or carry-on, or attach it to your person with an improved carabiner clip that sports a wider opening. The JBL Clip 5 has 12 hours of playtime on a single charge, is waterproof and dustproof, and can connect to other JBL Auracast-enabled speakers to get the party started when the plane lands.

Hotels and other vacation rentals promise fast Wi-Fi, maybe a microwave. But they are far less forthcoming with safety features. Which is why it can’t hurt to gift someone this packable, battery-powered CO monitor. It runs on two AA batteries and sounds an 85-decibel alarm when CO is detected. Whether someone you know is staying in the in-laws’ old farmhouse with a suspect furnace or a rustic cabin with a wood stove, this is a gift that fits next to the toiletries and covers the risk that alarms are missing or not working (just make sure to test it on arrival).

Every trip has that group photo that’s not the whole group, because someone has to hold the phone. Either that, or it’s framed weirdly because you have to lean the phone somewhere awkward to get everyone in frame. A JOBY GorillaPod stand solves that with its legs that bend and wrap around a railing, a tree branch … even bike handlebars. It’s lightweight and can hold more flagship smartphones up to 11.5 ounces and 2.2 to 3.6 inches wide, with or without a case. It can be positioned portrait or landscape, and has a standard mount so can even work with a small camera. It’s a great gift for that traveler who loves group shots, timelapse sunset shots, or just has to take a video call on the patio.

Capture travels, adventures, and precious moments in high fidelity with the $700 Insta360 X6 8K Camera. Dual custom-built Sony 1/1.1″ square sensors, a 4-nanometer AI chip that can make edits of your day’s adventures while you sleep, and two imaging chips create quality images and video that feel just like the IRL moment, and 140 minutes of battery runtime keeps the camera rolling for every moment on the itinerary. Built-in stabilization, windproof microphones, and waterproofing up to 65 feet help you capture all the action, wherever it is. This travel gift is excellent for the travel vlogger and adventure enthusiast who records trips for friends, family, and followers to enjoy.

There’s another type of travel we need to address: The Road Trip. And you can’t have a good road trip without a good soundtrack. If you know someone who wishes they could bop along to one of those enviable Dolby Atmos systems you find in luxury EVs, well, it’ll still cost $50K or more to do that thing where they walk out to a two-short-ton surprise in the driveway topped with a huge red bow. But if you want to get them the next-best thing at only $1,299, you can upgrade their (compatible) car’s receiver to the Pioneer SPHERA, the first aftermarket head unit to decode Atmos and virtualize it through your existing speakers using CarPlay (plus Apple Music, Apple Music Classical, and/or Audible). It will give them a taste of that sweet, sweet spatial audio but in a sensible sedan. The post-calibration time alignment, frequency response, and level adjustments put the driver and/or passengers in the center and create a perceptible dash-height channel from a nonexistent speaker. Backing vocals swelled from behind, and overall details take a step forward without feeling disconnected from the soundstage. Pioneer’s algorithms can even upmix stereo content and/or sculpt it with a 13-band EQ. No amount of reflections can match actual A-pillar and headliner speakers, but it’s an undeniably immersive upgrade to standard car stereo.

#4483. US battery storage just topped 200 GWh – here’s where it is

The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year.

Texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

Utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of new capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended.

“States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, New York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast.

The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%.

Solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often.

You wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms.

The article is good with the reporting about grid tied storage, but seems to miss the forest for the trees with it comes to pricing. Texas isn't installing more grid tied storage because of altruistic intent.

The storage is being added because they electricity suppliers can use it to make money. They can make money because we have a reasonably well thought out wholesale electrical market AND because that market has purchases large amounts of solar and wind generation.

That combination means that I still pay just $0.01 more per kwh than I did when I moved to this state 20 years ago. I pay 12 cents per kwh and Texas average is between 12 and 15. A functional market is what makes that work.

More than 300 solar and battery storage companies in the US wrote to Congress last week asking it to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty says the permitting bill would help get projects built faster and ease pressure on power prices. However, many Democrats feel this bill falls short. The Senate voted 70–27 on Monday to end debate on the amendment containing the bill’s text, moving it closer to a final vote.

#4482. Here’s How the Porsche 718 Boxster EV’s Fake Flat-Six and PDK Work

Porsche chose the 981-generation Boxster GTS model as its sound reference.

The upcoming Porsche 718 Boxster EV hops on board the growing simulated-internal-combustion-engine-and-transmission electric car trend. We just drove a prototype, and while there’s a lot to discuss about the car in general, it’s also worth honing in on the sound aspect. As you might expect, it’s rather pivotal to the experience behind the wheel.

The system that debuted in the Taycan is still called “E-Shift” here in the Boxster, and you can turn it on or off via a button on the steering wheel. Porsche chose the 3.4-liter naturally aspirated flat-six from the 981-generation Boxster as its muse. It’s a good choice, but also a bit of a surprise considering the spectacular sound out of the 4.0-liter flat-six found in the previous 718 Boxsters. But Porsche has its reasons, as Dr.-Ing. Sebastian Lefevre, team lead advanced driver assistance systems 718, tells us.

“It was a big discussion in our company,” Lefevre said. “From our point of view, the 4.0 engine is a little bit too soft in the sound. In our company, the 981 GTS sound, six-cylinder, was a little bit louder, and it would also feel more popular and familiar with our old customers.”

Once you hear the sound, there’s a good chance you’ll end up agreeing with Porsche. Lefevre mentioned the possibility of using the four-cylinder from the previous 718, but just as quickly shot the idea down referencing critique of the flat-four’s sound. How it reproduced the engine and exhaust via speakers is similar to how other OEMs with simulated internal combustion engines in EVs do it.

“A lot of microphones outside, inside,” Lefevre said. “And then we measured it all over the complete rpm range. And then we put it here, in this car, and measure it again. With the speakers, which are installed here. We have two.”

The most controversial speaker is bound to be the exterior-positioned one. More than anything, however, this exterior speaker exists as a sound maker for occupants to enjoy when the roof is off. It tries to emulate a mid-engine powertrain arrangement by way of the sound emanating from behind the driver and passenger; Porsche increases the volume inside the car with the roof removed, too. That’s a neat idea, but one that struggles to work in practice; I could hear some faint backfires on “downshifts” like Porsche’s ICE cars produce, but the experience is far from that of a real exhaust and engine echoing and reverberating off mountainsides or buildings.

Mercedes-AMG has the best ICE simulation around right now, with its AMG GT 4-Door Coupe going so far as to induce proper NVH characteristics by using exciters in the seats. The Boxster EV Prototype we drove relies entirely on the speakers to induce its hypnosis. But E-Shift brings a few theatrics to the table.

When lining up for a launch control start, Porsche pulses the torque of the electric motor to give a sense of an impending launch. It also lets you run the car into “redline,” tossing you forward with brake torque, just as it would in a manually-shifted gas-powered car. That said, Porsche took some liberties with the 8000-rpm redline depicted in this prototype; the 981 Boxster GTS instrument cluster shows a redline of 7600 rpm, so you have an extra 400 fake revs to play with in the EV.

Not as though this extra headroom matters, however, as Porsche chose to not simulate the torque curve of the flat-six. Instead, peak performance from the single electric motor is always available, and the car shuffles through its fake seven gears as speeds rise and fall. How it shifts is dependent on drive mode per usual with Porsche PDKs, and you can choose between manual or automatic shifting. You’ll even hear a tone difference in the engine noise over the speakers depending on whether you’re on- or off-throttle, just as you would were the real 3.4-liter be gulping in air behind your head.

For our full first impressions from behind the wheel of the 718 Boxster EV, make sure you read our prototype drive review.
