MSLA resin printers cure liquid photopolymer layer by layer with UV light.

Amazon has the Creality K2 Combo at $449, which is $197 under its $645.99 list price. The bundle pairs an enclosed CoreXY printer with a 260 x 260 x 260 mm build volume and one four-spool CFS unit, and Creality rates it for speeds up to 600 mm/s. The 16-color figure in Creality’s marketing takes four CFS units, so plan on four colors per print unless you buy three more.

The Adventurer 5M Pro is the pick here for someone who wants an enclosed printer for ABS or ASA and doesn’t need multi-color. It’s $359 at Amazon, down from a $479 list price. Flashforge lists a 220 x 220 x 220 mm build volume, a 280-degree Celsius quick-swap nozzle, a built-in camera, and a HEPA and carbon filter, and it rates quiet mode at 50 decibels. That build volume is smaller than the 260 mm cube on the K2 Combo above, so check the size of what you plan to print.

Resin is the way to go for miniatures and other small, detailed prints, and the Saturn 4 Ultra 12K is $399.99 at Amazon, a $194 cut from its $593.99 list price. It has a 10-inch 12K monochrome LCD and a tilting vat that peels each cured layer off the release film at an angle. Elegoo rates print speed at up to 150 mm/h. Budget for nitrile gloves, isopropyl alcohol, a wash and cure station, and a ventilated place to work, because resin printing needs all four. Elegoo also sells a 16K version with a sharper screen, so make sure you’re comparing the right model.

The other multi-color machines in this post top out at four colors without add-ons. The Kobra X Combo prints seven out of the box with Anycubic’s ACE 2 Pro filament box, and it’s $449.99 at Amazon (was $569.99). Its build volume is 260 x 260 x 260 mm, and Anycubic says the ACE 2 Pro dries filament at up to 65 degrees Celsius during a print. Reaching the advertised 19 colors takes four ACE 2 Pro units, and Anycubic warns against using cardboard spools in the box.

Bambu Lab’s own sale ends Dec. 1 at 2 a.m. Eastern and includes the dual-nozzle X2D, which succeeds the retired X1-Carbon.

These Amazon deals range from a $169 beginner bed slinger to a four-toolhead machine built to skip purge blocks.

For tabletop miniatures and display figures, MSLA resin printers still beat filament on fine detail.

Damp filament causes stringing and weak layer adhesion, and resin prints need an alcohol wash and UV cure before handling.

#4456. Man Allegedly Steals $150,000 Mercedes-Benz G-Wagen By Simply Asking for the Keys

A Florida woman reportedly returned to a hotel valet stand with her claim ticket, only to discover that someone else had already driven away in her luxury SUV.

Car thieves have become more sophisticated over the years. From key-cloning scanners to rerouting vehicle deliveries, criminals have found numerous ways to circumvent modern automotive security technology. But apparently, some thieves take a much simpler approach: they just politely ask for the keys. According to a Fox 13 Tampa Bay report, a Florida man is facing multiple criminal charges after allegedly convincing hotel valet attendants to hand over the keys to a $150,000 Mercedes-Benz G-Wagen that didn't belong to him.

Stella Stolper dropped off her Mercedes at the valet stand of the Marriott Waterside hotel in downtown Tampa at around 11 am on Friday, November 20. At about 4 p.m., she returned to the valet stand and presented her ticket. However, the valet attendants informed Stolper that her luxury SUV—which appears to be a Mercedes-AMG G63, based on footage provided to Fox 13 Tampa Bay—was already picked up a couple of hours earlier. That’s when the Tampa police got involved.

According to the police, the suspect convinced the valet attendants that the G-Wagen belonged to him, and he was ready to leave the hotel—so they handed him the keys, and off he went. He reportedly enjoyed a roughly three-hour joyride before police tracked down the Mercedes via GPS; shortly after 5 p.m., authorities say, the SUV was located and 28-year-old Payton Strain was arrested after a brief struggle. He is charged with grand theft auto, driving without a license, assault on a law enforcement officer and resisting an officer.

Stolper was thankful to have her vehicle back and that nobody was injured, and her Mercedes was returned without damage, although it apparently required some cleaning. However, she says she was also understandably baffled by the incident, questioning why the attendants hadn't verified the claim ticket against the keys before releasing such an expensive vehicle.

Having your car valeted at a hotel can be extremely convenient; just pull up to the entrance, hand over the keys, and continue with your day. Unfortunately, as this incident illustrates, it can be just as convenient for car thieves.

#4455. Hyundai claims 2027’s ‘Best EV Brand’ title as the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 impress

Hyundai’s electric SUVs are getting some love. The IONIQ 5 and three-row IONIQ 9 helped the Korean automaker land its first-ever “Best Electric Vehicle Brand” award from US News & World Report for 2027.

“This win showcases the breadth and strength of Hyundai’s SUV and electric lineups,” Alex Kwanten, managing editor at Autos at US News, said after naming it the Best EV Brand and Best SUV Brand for 2027.

This marks the first time Hyundai has earned the Best EV Brand award and the third consecutive win for Best SUV Brand.

Including hybrid and electric vehicles, Hyundai offers ten unique SUVs, “many of them at or near the top of our rankings in those classes for capability, comfort, performance and value,” Kwanten said.

Hyundai’s fully electric SUVs, the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9, “in particular, stand out for their combination of style and technology,” he explained.

Hyundai currently offers the IONIQ 5, including the sporty IONIQ 5 N and off-road-focused IONIQ 5 XRT, plus the three-row IONIQ 9.

Although Hyundai discontinued its electric sedan, the IONIQ 6, after the 2025 model year, the new high-performance IONIQ 6 N joins the lineup in 2027.

The IONIQ 5 continued to earn praise, taking its third consecutive Best Compact Electric SUV award. Its larger sibling, the IONIQ 9, took the top spot in the midsize electric SUV category.

Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in the US this year through September that isn’t a Tesla, ranking third behind the Model Y and Model 3.

Why does it continue winning over buyers? The IONIQ 5 checks all the boxes with long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior with modern tech.

It’s also among the most affordable EVs in the US. Prices for the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 start at just $35,250.

However, the base price is for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model costs an extra $2,500, with prices starting at $37,750, but it offers up to 318 miles of range.

The three-row Hyundai IONIQ 9 electric SUV starts at $58,955 with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles.

Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is about the size of a Tesla Model Y, with two rows of seating and space for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating with six- or seven-seat options.

The larger IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with up to 106.5 cubic feet in the IONIQ 5.

Both electric SUVs use an 800-volt electrical architecture for ultra-fast charging. The IONIQ 5 can charge from 10% to 80% in about 20 minutes, while the IONIQ 9 takes around 24 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Hyundai assembles the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.

When we toured the facility earlier this year, Hyundai told Electrek that its electric SUVs are winning over new buyers at a higher rate than any of its gas or hybrid vehicles.

The IONIQ 5 had a 69.8% conquest rate last year, while the IONIQ 9 had 64.3%. Hyundai’s Elantra N ranked third (61.9%), followed by the Palisade (61.2%) and Kona Electric (60.9%).

Is Hyundai the best Electric Vehicle brand in your opinion? While Hyundai took the top spot overall, Lucid remained the Best Luxury EV Brand for the second consecutive year. Hyundai’s Genesis also repeated as Best Luxury Brand. Share your thoughts in the comments below.

The sale includes a laptop power bank with dual 140W USB-C ports for less than $45 and Qi2 magnetic packs for less than $30. Every link below goes straight to an individual Amazon product page.

Two specs matter before you buy a travel battery. The FAA caps carry-on lithium batteries at 100 watt-hours without airline approval, which works out to roughly 27,000mAh, and power banks always belong in your carry-on bag instead of checked luggage. If you want to charge a modern laptop, look for at least 65W of USB-C Power Delivery output, and 100W to 140W for larger machines. For snap-on phone packs, Qi2 certification means 15W wireless charging (25W on newer Qi2.2 packs).

This is the pack to start with if you want laptop-grade output without laptop-grade pricing. Amazon has it down to $44.33 from its $85.99 list price, which is 48 percent off. EcoFlow lists two 140W USB-C ports, a 25,000mAh capacity, and a display that shows what the pack is doing. The trade-off is the 170W total: one laptop can pull full speed, but two power-hungry machines will split the output. If you need more headroom, the EcoFlow Rapid Pro is rated for 300W and costs $89.99.

UGREEN’s 130W Nexode is $54.99 at Amazon, down from a $89.99 list price (39 percent off). The listing describes three ports, PD 3.0 charging, and a TFT display for checking charge status at a glance. UGREEN rates it at 72Wh, so it sits comfortably below the 100Wh carry-on limit. You give up some capacity compared with the 25,000mAh packs further down. The 25,000mAh, 145W Nexode is only $5 more at $59.98 if you’d rather have the extra capacity.

A magnetic pack makes the most sense when you don’t want to think about a cable at all. This Qi2-certified Anker snaps onto MagSafe-compatible iPhones and charges wirelessly at up to 15W. Amazon has it for $62.99, which is 21 percent off its $79.99 list price. A 10,000mAh pack adds real bulk to the back of a phone, though. If pocketability matters more than capacity, the 5,000mAh Anker Nano Qi2 pack is $42.99 and Anker lists it at 0.34 inches thick.

The Prime is the splurge pick, and at $119.99 it’s 33 percent off its $179.99 list price at Amazon. Anker rates it for 220W of total output across three ports, with two-way charging so the pack refills quickly, plus app control. That’s enough to run a laptop and still fast-charge a phone and tablet. Know that this version doesn’t include Anker’s charging base, and that you’re paying a premium for output most phone-only users won’t use.

These higher-output USB-C packs are built to charge a laptop, a handheld gaming PC, or several devices at once.

These packs snap onto the back of a MagSafe-compatible phone and charge it wirelessly.

These hybrids fold out a wall plug, so one device works as both a charger and a battery.

These 5,000mAh to 20,000mAh packs handle phone, earbud, and tablet top-ups, and many have a cable built in.

These three are built for specific jobs: backpacking, bad weather, and the Nintendo Switch 2.

#4450. Ford Has A Dedicated Battery Abuse Team. It Obsesses Over How Cells Fail

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Electric vehicle batteries live a harder life than the ones in your phone or laptop. They spend most of their time outdoors, deal with extreme heat and cold, and can take a beating from road debris and potholes.

That means for battery makers, engineering for durability is a priority right up there with energy density and charging speed. And to make sure its cells can handle the abuse of daily life as an EV, Ford has a team dedicated to understanding how batteries fail—and how to stop it.

“That team is 100% focused on battery abuse, design, and testing as a function,” Wesley Thibault, the global chief engineer of battery product development at Ford said last week during a media roundtable at the automaker’s new battery plant in Marshall, Michigan.

Ford is new to the EV battery business. Last week, it started cranking out lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, using technology licensed from China’s CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. The batteries will power the all-important Ford Fathom pickup, which the automaker says will enter production toward the end of next year and kick off a new generation of vastly better and more profitable EVs.

Despite the licensing deal, Ford officials said they were involved in developing the batteries from the outset, with a focus on durability.

The job is not as simple as it sounds. The battery abuse team isn’t tasked with destroying fully made cells and then finding ways to make them indestructible. Instead, Thibault said, it is involved in the design process from the start.

“They want to understand down to the physics level, how a cell fails and why, and when it does fail, how we can prevent it from creating harm to the occupants,” he said.

Quality operator at Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan.

For example, the team measures how cells vent, a crucial process that keeps batteries from catching fire or damaging themselves when they overheat. When temperatures inside a cell get too high, the electrolyte, the liquid chemical that shuttles electrons between the anode and cathode, gets hot and releases gases.

If those gases stay trapped, they can cause short circuits or thermal runaway, so they need to escape in a controlled way. Thibault said his team can measure all of this analytically—using computer models—before the cells are validated.

Production adds another layer of scrutiny. At various stages, the materials inside the cell, as well as the finished cell itself, go through thousands of quality checks, Ford engineers said. Those include CT scans, X-ray machines, lasers, camera inspections, and AI systems.

For example, when the anode slurry is coated onto a copper foil, every millimeter is scanned by lasers for wrinkles and other anomalies. All employees have the ability to pause production if they spot any problems.In case of any issues, they quarantine the cells affected during a specific time period. Ford also claimed that impacted components can be traced all the way from production to the vehicle they end up in.

To be sure, not all of this is unique to Ford. Strict quality checks like these are common among major battery makers, who all aim to minimize scrap rates for costly batteries and maximize the amount of material that actually gets sold.

Ford engineer operating a winding machine, which brings together the anode and cathode, adding a separator in between.

Ford continuously tests the manufacturing process in other ways, too. Engineers said they intentionally feed damaged components and cells—which they call “red rabbits”—into the production machinery to confirm the quality systems catch them and are working as intended.

When cells are almost ready, they’re blasted with helium gas to check for leaks. Once a pack is assembled, it’s mounted on a hydraulic shaker that mimics thousands of miles and years of real-world road use. The shaker can twist, dive, squat, contort, yaw, and replicate the other movements of a car, putting the pack through everything it would see on the road.

Ford’s EV batteries have fared well, by and large. High-mileage Mach-Es with 100,000 or even 200,000 miles on the odometer show little range loss compared to their original capacity, according to data the company released this month.

On the other hand, Ford’s emphasis on battery quality isn’t exactly surprising. The company has grappled with high warranty costs in recent years. And both the Mustang Mach-E and the F-150 Lightning have had issues linked to their high-voltage batteries. Some early Mach-Es were recalled because their battery contactors would overheat during DC fast-charging. A small number of Lightnings were recalled in 2023 due to defective battery cells.

Ford will want to avoid any similar quality issues as it rolls out the high-stakes Fathom, which it hopes will outsell its previous EVs and set the stage for an electric comeback. It will be years before we know how the Fathom's batteries hold up in the real world. For now, it looks like the company is pulling out all the stops to make sure things go off without a hitch.

#4449. This Watch Dropped the Beat for the Funky Aughts

Louis Vuitton’s first timepiece remains the heart of its lineup.

Louis Vuitton Horlogerie Tambour Automatic 40 mm in Rose Gold, $65,000, louisvuitton.com

Inspiration can come from the most unlikely of sources. If any era could be defined by that fact, it would be the early Aughts. During this transitional period, watch brands young and old looked to establish themselves within an emerging luxury space, and they did so in wildly diverse and creative ways. Before the throwback trend took hold of the industry, design language was largely forward-looking with an emphasis on innovation and character. This was the scene in 2002, when Louis Vuitton entered the watch market with the unconventional Tambour, which has since served as the core of the brand’s efforts in this domain.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

Taking its name from the French word for “drum,” the original Tambour watch features towering walls that widen at the base and accept an integrated lug piece reminiscent of the brand’s luggage handles. A reverence to the craft is clear from subtle details such as the alignment of the Louis Vuitton letters along the side of the case matching each hour marker, the shape of the crown and pushers, and the articulation of the lug. The drumlike case remains unique to this day, and the Tambour template has proved surprisingly versatile, with Louis Vuitton expanding the collection into a range of styles.

The Tambour stands as a monument to the best elements of its formative era and remains one of the Aughts’ more enduring horological identities. Today’s modern iteration is a refined reflection of the same ideas that put Louis Vuitton on the timekeeping map nearly a quarter ­century ago. The funky Aughts freedom that allowed for the creation of the Tambour turned into a core strength for a 21st-century watchmaking powerhouse.

#4447. Kia’s cheapest EV is coming next year, and it could cost under $25,000

Kia’s EV lineup covers just about every size and price point, but it believes one thing is still missing: a truly cheap electric car. That’s about to change in 2027, when Kia plans to unveil a new EV that could start at around $22,000 to $24,000.

It’s been 40 years since Kia introduced its first electric vehicle, the Besta EV, created so runners in the 1986 Asian Games wouldn’t have to breathe toxic fumes from the broadcast vehicle.

Kia has come a long way since the Besta EV hit the road, now offering a complete lineup of electric vehicles, from compact SUVs and hatchbacks to vans and three-row SUVs.

In Europe and the UK, Kia’s electric lineup consists of the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 van, but the Korean automaker isn’t done yet.

“With no intention of resting on its laurels,” Kia said, the brand plans to complete development of its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) by the end of 2027, an all-new B-segment EV hatchback.

It didn’t offer any other details on the upcoming EV, but Ted Lee, Kia’s executive vice president and head of global operations, told Auto Express that Kia and Hyundai are co-developing a new dedicated EV architecture for an upcoming pair of entry-level electric cars.

Expected to arrive as the Hyundai IONIQ 1 and Kia EV1, the new EVs will compete with other entry-level electric cars like the Renault Twingo, which starts at about €20,000.

Lee said the EV1’s price will be highly competitive not just with other entry-level EVs, but also with small gas-powered cars, with prices expected to start in the €20,000 to €22,000 range, or about $22,000 to $24,000. And that’s without government incentives.

The EV2 starts at just €26,600 ($29,500) in Germany and other European markets as Kia’s current entry-level EV, so the price range would make sense.

While it will be Kia’s cheapest EV, Lee promised it would not cut corners in quality, design, or features.

As its first SDV, the EV1 will feature Kia and Hyundai Motor’s latest-generation tech and software. Kia said the electric SDV will offer Level 2+ autonomous driving on highways. In 2029, Kia plans to expand to Level 2++, enabling it to operate in cities.

The new EV will also use Hyundai’s SDV architecture (CODA), the Pleos Connect infotainment system, and Gleo AI, an in-vehicle Agenic AI.

What will the EV1 look like? According to Auto Express, the entry-level EV will look a bit sportier and less boxy than the EV2 SUV. It could draw inspiration from the Vision Meta Turismo concept.

It also apparently won’t be based on the Picanto, Kia’s smallest gas-powered car. The Kia EV1 is expected to bring a unique style to the family.

This is good to see and makes sense, especially in Europe. I don't think Kia can go wrong making vehicles at so many different price points. It allows them to reach different segments and almost literally have something for almost everyone.

While all of Kia’s current EVs feature its ccNC infotainment system with dual 12.3″ instrument display and infotainment screens, plus a 5″ climate control panel, the EV1 could bring a simpler setup.

Like its other electric models, the EV1 is expected to receive the GT treatment. However, as an entry-level model, it may not use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive setup like the others.

Will Kia bring the EV1 to the US? Don’t get your hopes up. Kia has previously said the B-segment hatchback is designed for Europe. It could even be built alongside the EV2 at Kia’s plant in Slovakia.

The good news? The EV3, Kia’s compact electric SUV, is now on sale in the US, starting at just $29,890.

#4446. VW’s Cheap EVs Are So Popular, Buyers Face Wait Times Of Nearly Two Years

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volkswagen, along with its group siblings, Skoda and Seat, are facing huge demand for their small electric cars, which in turn is leading to wait times that are nearing two years in some cases.

With over 50,000 orders on tap already, the Volkswagen ID. Polo hatchback is one of the most successful models from the Volkswagen Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family, with the most affordable trim having wait times of up to 21 months in Germany, according to Spanish outlet Motor.es. That’s double compared to the 10-month wait times reported earlier this year.

Cupra Raval and Volkswagen ID. Polo production in Martorell, Spain

It’s a similar story when it comes to the technically similar Skoda Epiq, with over 80,000 orders since its introduction and wait times of up to 17 months for the most popular versions. The Cupra Raval, meanwhile, has amassed roughly 50,000 orders and has faced a multi-day production halt at the Martorell plant in Spain, where it shares an assembly line with the ID. Polo.

Together, the four models that make up the group’s affordable EV family, namely the Volkswagen ID. Polo, the Cupra Raval, the Skoda Epiq, and the Volkswagen ID. Cross, have attracted approximately 150,000 orders in Europe since their debut through the end of September.

It’s worth noting that while the cheap trims of all these cars, which start at around €24,995 ($27,300) in Germany, have put the Volkswagen Group in an unfavorable position, the more expensive versions are scheduled to ship a lot faster. The ID. Polo Sportline currently has a five-month wait time, while customers of the ID. Polo GTI have to wait roughly seven months.

The higher-than-expected demand has put all automakers at the mercy of battery cell suppliers. Currently, the Martorell factory that assembles the ID. Polo and Cupra Raval is working double shifts and has a daily output of up to 1,000 vehicles, but work has already begun to add a third shift, which would increase output to 1,200 vehicles daily.

The expansion is tied to battery production, and while there’s a factory nearby that can build up to 1,200 packs per day, it relies on cells that come from an external supplier. The same goes for the Pamplona plant that assembles the Volkswagen ID. Cross and Skoda Epiq electric crossovers. The two EVs share the same assembly line as VW’s combustion-powered T-Cross and Taigo, both of which bring in more money than their battery-powered counterparts.

A Volkswagen spokesperson told Germany's Automobilwoche that demand has increased “significantly more dynamically than originally expected” and that ramping up production “cannot be adjusted short-term to the same extent as this dynamically increasing demand.”

More employees are being added to the workforce, and Gotion’s new cell factory in Spain is expected to be fully operational early next year, which should help the automaker boost production without relying on outside help.

The Han EV will offer two single-motor rear-wheel-drive (RWD) options, with an output of 328 hp (245 kW) and 402 hp (300 kW). A dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) version will also be offered, delivering a combined 697 hp (520 kW).

The PHEV version, on the other hand, uses a 1.5-liter engine and an electric motor with up to 268 hp (200 kW).

Ahead of its expected debut at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27, BYD’s new Han was captured in public without any disguise.

The images sent to Autohome show a design similar to the Great Han and other new Dynasty series vehicles, with its latest “Dragon Face” signature front-end look.

A few things have changed from the current model, including new headlights and a full-length light bar, while the Chinese symbol moved to the hood.

From the side, the Han features a sleek, fastback silhouette. The vehicle also features a roof-mounted LiDAR to support advanced driver-assistance features. The new Han is expected to feature BYD’s God’s Eye B ADAS system.

Inside, the new Han adopts BYD’s updated interior design. The new setup includes a floating center infotainment screen and a digital instrument panel behind a three-spoke steering wheel.

The center console is also updated with two wireless phone chargers and cupholders without covers.

Doesn't matter for us here in the USA (for now), but I wish the back was a little more sedan looking with a little more trunk lid. Otherwise, nice car.

BYD’s new Han is 5,156 mm long, 1,969 mm wide, and 1,507 mm tall, with a wheelbase of 3,030 mm, which is 161 mm longer than the current version.

The flagship Great Han is the largest of the series, measuring 5,256 mm long. After launching the Great Han on October 13, BYD sold 4,000 units by November 1.

Since the flagship sedan starts at 235,900 yuan, or about $35,000, the smaller Han will likely be closer to 200,000 yuan ($30,000) or less. The outgoing Han starts at 168,800 yuan ($25,000).

#4442. BMW Can't Build Its New iX3 Fast Enough. Now It's Adding The iX4

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BMW can barely keep up with demand for the iX3 electric crossover, and it’s already adding a second model at its new plant in Debrecen, Hungary. After getting over 100,000 orders in Europe for the iX3, the coupe-like iX4 has started rolling off the assembly line alongside its more conventional-looking sibling.

The move comes after several record-setting performances from BMW. The new facility in Debrecen, the first one that started churning out Neue Klasse-based EVs, went down in history for the fastest production ramp of any new BMW Group factory, with just eight months needed to achieve mass production at a sustained pace.

The second and third shifts were added ahead of schedule to keep up with the higher-than-expected demand for the iX3, and the plant has been running around the clock since September. Since early November, the factory has added the iX4 to its lineup, boosting its output even further.

But it’s not just the Neue Klasse crossovers that have enjoyed success. The new i3, which has nothing in common with the quirky first-generation electric hatchback, has seen high demand, prompting the automaker to open the order books in Europe earlier than originally planned. What’s more, the historic plant in Munich that has made gas-powered cars for all of its existence has been converted to build EVs, marking a big shift right at the heart of the Bavarian manufacturer.

Separately, the new iX5, which is not based on the Neue Klasse architecture but borrows a lot of tech from the new platform, has started rolling off the line in Spartanburg, South Carolina, marking the beginning of EV manufacturing in the United States for BMW.

Getting back to the iX4, the start of production means that the first customers should start receiving their cars sooner rather than later, including those in the U.S. In fact, U.S.-spec iX4s are among the first to roll off the line in Hungary. Based on the same underpinnings as the massively successful iX3, the coupe-like EV boasts an EPA-estimated range of 428 miles and a dual-motor powertrain that develops a combined 463 horsepower.

The 112.2-kilowatt-hour battery can be charged from a DC stall at up to 400 kilowatts, with a 10-minute session resulting in up to 183 miles of range added, which is just one mile short compared to the technically similar iX3 50 xDrive. On AC power, the iX4 can accept up to 15.4 kW.

The 2027 BMW iX4 50 xDrive, the only one that’s on sale right now, starts at $66,200 plus destination.

#4441. Alpitronic’s new SC plant to build 400 kW and 1 MW fast chargers

Alpitronic, the company behind IONNA’s fast chargers, is investing nearly $34 million in a new South Carolina factory. It’ll build 400 kW DC fast chargers, plus a 1 megawatt (MW) system that can charge cars and heavy-duty trucks.

The $33.94 million project in Fort Mill is expected to create 70 jobs, the South Carolina Department of Commerce announced Wednesday. It’ll be the Bolzano, Italy-based Alpitronic’s first operation in South Carolina, just across the state line from its North American headquarters in Charlotte.

The HYC400 packs up to 400 kW into a single unit. If you’ve stopped at an IONNA Rechargery, you may have already plugged into one.

The HYC1000 works differently. A separate power cabinet can send up to 1 MW across as many as eight vehicles at once, shifting power between them as their charging needs change. Operators can configure it with CCS or NACS plugs for passenger EVs or a Megawatt Charging System (MCS) plug for compatible heavy-duty trucks.

Alpitronic’s 400 kW chargers were already being made in Wisconsin for Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging in 2024. Alpitronic Americas CEO Patrik Herrnegger said the Fort Mill plant “will put US production under our direct control, bring us closer to our customers, and enable us to serve them more efficiently.”

The 173,315-square-foot site at 3560 Stateview Blvd. (pictured above) will also house a testing lab, repair operations, a warehouse, logistics space, and offices. South Carolina approved job development credits and awarded York County a $200,000 grant to help pay for building improvements.

How do their production costs compare to Supercharger stalls, and what's their yearly production rate capacity? I only called out Supercharger cost comparisons because SC's are well known to be the cheapest in the industry to produce.

Alpitronic expects to start operations in February 2027.

#4440. Porsche Patents Steering Wheel With Rim That Grows Thicker for Spirited Driving

No, your 911 isn’t just happy to see you.

Sporty cars face a conundrum with their steering wheels. A thick steering wheel and giant paddle shifters are very handy when wielding the car at its limits on track, but that same wheel can be annoying and cumbersome overkill for an everyday commute ... which, let’s face it, is what most people are doing with their BMW M vehicles.

Porsche, however, has a potential solution to the problem—one guaranteed to generate all kinds of puerile puns. As website CarMoses recently uncovered, a recent German patent filing from Porsche provides details for a shape-shifting steering wheel, which can enlarge and reduce the thickness of its rim at the push of a button.

The patented Porsche steering wheel contains two elements. One is a hydraulic system that expands and deflates certain sections of the wheel rim for enhanced grip; a stretchy Alcantara material would accommodate the wheel’s, er, tumescence. The other element is paddle shifters on either spoke that would expand when needed in concert with the wheel, and retract when not in use. When deployed, the system would give the driver greater contact patch for their hands during aggressive driving, be it steering or shifting.

The wheel rim and paddle shifters could deploy automatically by shifting into a sporty driving mode, or manually with the push of a button. Drivers wishing for their Porsche to appear happy to see them could also have the wheel thickening deploy through a pre-set driver profile. The patent also notes that the wheel rim’s hydraulic system could have an additional temperature-regulation function; it could double as a heater for the wheel in cold weather, or cool the wheel on track.

Keep in mind, automakers patent many features that are unlikely to make it to production. (Don’t expect to drive standing up in your Ford Bronco anytime soon.) But the expanding and retracting steering wheel feels like it could be useful in future Porsches, if the brand can work out safety concerns and add it in a reasonably cost-effective manner. That said, the feature would, alas, provide a clear visual indicator that would make slyly slipping the car into a sportier driving mode on a curvy road while your partner isn’t paying attention a bit more difficult to hide.

#4439. The 2027 Cadillac Vistiq Gets A Price Bump And More Options

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The 2027 Cadillac Vistiq just got a little more expensive, as spotted by GM Authority. For the latest iteration of the relatively young three-row electric SUV that slots under the huge Escalade IQ, Cadillac wants between $900 and $1,000 more than a month ago.

The higher starting price doesn’t necessarily mean more equipment, though the Vistiq now comes with a native Tesla-style NACS charging port, just like all the other 2027 EVs made by General Motors.

That said, the automaker is not throwing in any complimentary adapters, so owners who want a manufacturer-approved DC fast-charging adapter to use at CCS stalls will have to shell out an extra $189, even if they opt for the top-spec Platinum trim that starts at roughly $100,000.

For what it’s worth, Cadillac is offering a charging adapter bundle that includes a CCS1 adapter and an AC adapter for J1772 stations for a total of $256, which is quite good value for money.

Compared to the 2026 Vistiq, the 2027 model brings two new optional appearance packages and a few new exterior paint colors. The Onyx Package, which is only available on the top Platinum trim, comes with 23-inch black wheels, gloss black nameplates, Obsidian Chrome mirror caps, and puddle lamps that depict the Cadillac logo. Then, there’s the Onyx Lite package, which can be had on the Sport trim only. It features all of the goodies in the big Onyx pack, except the 23-inch wheels.

As standard, the 2027 Cadillac Vistiq comes with 21-inch Bright Silver alloy wheels, a dual-motor powertrain capable of outputting 615 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque, and a 102-kilowatt-hour battery that enables a maximum EPA-estimated range of 305 miles.

The Luxury and Sport trims come standard with an 11.5-kW on-board charger, while the Premium Luxury and Platinum trims come standard with an upgraded on-board charger capable of accepting up to 19.2 kW from a Level 2 dispenser. The uprated on-board charger can be spec’d on the first two trims, too, but it costs an additional $1,480.

For 2027, the Luxury and Premium Luxury trims cost $900 more than the outgoing model, while the Sport and Platinum trims are now $1,000 more expensive than before. As a result, the 2027 Cadillac Vistiq now starts at $80,395, while the top trim’s MSRP is now $99,495.

All trims get the same powertrain, but the more expensive versions come with more kit as standard.

#4438. NSSL keeps growing its electric terminal truck fleet, with no plans to stop

After taking delivery of its first Orange EV e-Triever electric yard tractor in 2024, NSSL saw the electric light. The company has been moving quickly to transition its yard tractor fleet to zero emissions, and its efforts haven’t gone unnoticed: NSSL is now being recognized by the 2026 Canadian Clean Fleet Awards.

Toronto’s National Shunt Service, Ltd. (NSSL) added its first electric terminal truck to its trailer-moving operations back in 2024 – and they were impressed enough to quickly start buying more, putting their Orange e-Triever and Husk-e trucks to work at customers’ warehouses, distribution centers, and factories. The company has 42 electric trucks working at a number of sites in Canada (up from 27 in June), with plans to have 50 by the end of Q1 2027.

“(Electric is) part of every customer conversation we’re having today,” says Darren Fitzgerald, NSSL’s chief commercial officer. “If customers aren’t asking about electrification, we are bringing it to the conversation.”

The company’s commitment to decarbonization recently made them a 2026 Canadian Clean Fleets Award winner, recognizing their growing role in normalizing battery-electric, zero-emission commercial trucks across Canada.

NSSL used Geotab telematics to track pertinent data of each vehicle, giving what Fitzgerald called, “an essential overview of the entire fleet,” that enabled the company to compare efficiencies and cost, as well as the ability to plan ahead.

“The data allows us to identify potential maintenance issues before they result in an outage,” he explains. “Just as importantly, it gives us the analytics to understand idle time, fuel and energy consumption, utilization, and overall operating efficiency.”

If NSSL’s experience is anything like many, many, many others, they’ll find that the case for electrification is stronger than ever.

#4437. General Motors Futureliner #7 Has a New Lease On Life. Its Restorers Plan to Use It

After its starring role at the 2026 Retromobile New York show, Matt Katz and Rob Ida have big road trip plans for the 1939 Futureliner.

In 1941, General Motors hit the open road with its fleet of Futureliners on the Parade of Progress, a movement meant to spread cutting-edge science and technology across America. With their bubble-top cockpits, exhibition-style innards, and shining chrome panels, the Futureliners became as much of a spectacle as the displays on automotive technology, urban engineering, farming, and leisure pursuits carried within. Now, 85 years later, a resurrected Futureliner is carrying the Parade of Progress torch into the 21st Century—starting in New York City.

Like many modern automotive stories, this Futureliner's resurrection began on Facebook Marketplace. When Matt Katz, owner of the Caretakers Collection, was sent a link to an available Futureliner on the online classified site, he jumped into action. Katz was on the phone with the seller in a matter of minutes, and quickly deputized friend and New Jersey car builder Rob Ida to travel up to Massachusetts the following day.

“[The seller] was totally caught off guard that I just called him. He's like, ‘Listen, like it's Monday night. I'm out at an event. You know, call me tomorrow.’ I'm like, ‘No, no, no, I want to make this deal now.’ I just wanted to lock it up,” Katz said to Road & Track. He said he informed the seller that he wanted Ida, with whom Katz had done prior restoration projects, to come check out the Futureliner. “I was like, ‘Let me call [Ida] and get him to come out and inspect it within forty-eight hours. And if all is good, I'll wire you the balance. And if all is not, return the money to me, the deposit, and we'll call it even.’”

Ida reported back that the Futureliner example was ripe for restoration, but the journey couldn’t begin immediately. First, Ida had to cut a larger opening in his garage to fit the Futureliner through. Standing 11-feet-7-inches tall and 33 feet long, the GM Futureliner is taller than your average school bus, and about as long as an average fire truck. But once the Futureliner had been transported and maneuvered into Ida’s garage, the real work began.

As it had been owned and restored by the Peter Pan Bus Company in the 1990s, this Futureliner build started out in better shape than most. It had been updated with GM’s post-World War II styling from 1953—a flatter and less regal version of the shape introduced in 1939. Ida and Katz wanted to bring this Futureliner back to its original Harley Earl-designed glory, but there wasn’t an official blueprint to guide them. Ida even reached out to the General Motors Heritage Center, but it had limited information available about the first-generation Futureliner design. So, Ida had to fabricate many of the parts himself. Some era-specific parts even required the creation of bespoke molds, as no replacements were available.

“We work off imagery, and we work off of any kind of text or information that we can find. Unfortunately, the Thirty-Nine version is much more difficult to find than the Fifty-Three version. Anytime you do a quick search, you're going to find all the white roof Fifty-Three generation-two post-war Futureliner. So that was really the difficult part: digging deep enough to find the Thirty-Nine version,” Ida said to Road & Track.

“Somewhere in a conversation with Rob, it came to be that we both agreed: let's go back to the bubble. Let's bring it back to Thirty-Nine, and we didn't realize and truly fully appreciate what that meant. Getting the bubble done was just difficult, but we knew what to do, and Rob had experience,” Katz said. “We didn't realize that after we made that decision, everything else would change on the bus. Not just the paint colors, but also the cladding on the side. So, Fifty-Three has seven clads; ours is four. The GM logo on the front. Rob randomly found this old video by a production company called Rose that I discovered, and he poured through it and discovered in a small clip that the GM logo was backlit.”

Once the restoration was complete, Katz and Ida were eager to show off the piece of moving history, and the inaugural Retromobile event in New York City was the perfect venue. But the newly revived Futureliner had to make it from Old Bridge, New Jersey, to Manhattan’s Jacob K. Javits Convention Center. There is no shortage of driving obstacles between those two points on a good day in a regular car, so piloting the massive machine was sure to be a challenge—but with Ida and Katz at the helm, however, the journey went smoother than expected. Thanks to dually-style front wheels, power steering, 360-degree cameras, and working air conditioning, driving the Futureliner was an exercise in patience more than anything else.

“So I drove from Columbus Circle to Times Square to Javits. And as a New Yorker, driving it in New York and just seeing people's reactions ... you know, part of the enjoyment is how people react to it. I've never had a reaction like when I was driving it. And then the fact that they closed Times Square for me while we were driving, and for Rob and me ... I couldn't even have fathomed that as a dream,” Katz said.

And the Futureliner’s adventures are far from over. Katz and Ida are currently scheming a cross-country road trip, starting on the East Coast in 2027 and heading west toward GM’s Heritage Center in Sterling, Michigan. After that, the Futureliner will head to California for the 2027 Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance, with stops at dealerships and historical markers along the way. The Futureliner will then spend some time at the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles and stick around for the 2028 Summer Olympics before heading back to GM’s Heritage Center. This cross-country journey will be focused on charity efforts for organizations like the Sloan Kettering Institute for Cancer Research, which the original Parade of Progress highlighted. Trust us: if the Futureliner comes to your town, it’s worth seeing in person.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4436. GM’s V2G pilot wants to pay California drivers for power from parked EVs

GM Energy and WeaveGrid are launching a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) pilot that will let select Southern California Edison (SCE) customers send electricity from their EV batteries back to the grid. Eligible drivers could get more than $16,000 in help with equipment and installation, and earn money when the grid needs their power.

GM says the pilot participants will be its first EV drivers in California to export power from their cars to their homes. Through the California Energy Commission, eligible customers in SCE’s Emergency Load Reduction Program can get up to $8,000 toward a GM Energy V2H system and up to $8,099 toward eligible installation costs, including connecting the system to the grid.

Chevy, GMC, and Cadillac EV drivers can use time-of-use energy management to take advantage of lower rates and may be paid for participating in eligible demand-response events. How much they save or earn depends on their rate plan, electricity use, and participation.

GM already offers managed charging through 13 utilities, and each program varies by utility.

An EV battery stores direct current (DC), and your house and the grid use alternating current (AC). GM’s current home backup system uses a wall-mounted inverter to convert the power. With AC bidirectional charging, the car’s onboard inverter does the job. Moving that work into the car could make the equipment on your garage wall simpler and cheaper to install.

Not in CA, but we use solar, time of use, and EVs to minimize our energy costs. We’re not feeding power back to the grid from our cars, but the combo of TOU, solar and EVs does allow us to reduce costs significantly. Solar covers all the expensive peak power, I have the cars start charging early enough to use any extra solar, and the rest is off peak at half cost.

GM is joining CharIN‘s North American AC V2G task force, which is working to align technical standards, equipment certification, and utility approval requirements. In Southern California, the pilot will give GM and its partners a look at how the process works for drivers, from signing up and getting the hardware installed to getting utility approval and sending power back.

#4435. Lucid Gravity Robotaxis Just Took A Major Step Toward Commercial Launch

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Lucid has its sights set on America’s burgeoning autonomous-vehicle ecosystem, and now it's one important step closer to getting robotaxis on the road. The California electric vehicle startup, along with Uber and self-driving technology company Nuro, has started testing driverless Gravity SUVs in the San Francisco Bay Area, the companies announced Tuesday.

More than 100 Gravitys have already been testing on public roads in San Francisco and Houston since January, but every one of them had a human supervisor in the driver's seat. Taking the safety operator out of the vehicle is a major step ahead of the service's planned commercial launch in the Bay Area in the first quarter of 2027.

The stakes are high for Lucid. The luxury automaker has burned through billions and struggled to meaningfully scale up its vehicle sales of the Air and Gravity. Increasingly, it's turning to the growing robotaxi market for a new source of sales volume and revenue. It plans to deploy tens of thousands of robotaxis in the U.S. and Europe.

If things go to plan, Lucid, Uber, and Nuro will join Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox as the few companies offering truly driverless paid ride-hailing in the U.S. Unlike those rivals, which offer rides through their own dedicated apps, the Gravity will be available through Uber. Uber has set out to become the go-to platform for driverless vehicles, and has struck deals to put Waymo and Zoox taxis on its app in certain cities. Uber's exclusivity deal with Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, however, will end in 2028 as the Alphabet-owned company plans to shift to its own app in those cities.

Lucid said initial phase of on-road driverless testing will take place in Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale. More Bay Area cities will be added next year. A fleet of more than 100 Gravitys are included in these driverless tests, all of which have hardware and software upgrades compared to those in the previous phase of testing.

On paper, the Gravity has some advantages over its competitors. It is among the longest-range and fastest-charging electric SUVs in the U.S., with up to 450 miles of range on a single charge and 400-kilowatt charging that can add 200 miles in as little as 11 minutes. That should mean fewer charging stops and less downtime, which could potentially keep the vehicle earning fares for longer.

Lucid Gravity robotaxi commercial roadmap.

It will also have to maintain a high utilization rate to recover its steep starting price, which begins at $81,750 for the passenger version without any autonomous hardware and software. (Lucid hasn’t said how much the robotaxi version costs, or how much the extra weight affects range and efficiency.)

The Gravity isn’t Lucid’s only vehicle that will someday do robotaxi duty. The upcoming midsize platform will also spawn a robotaxi, although Lucid hasn’t said if it will be a version of the Cosmos or something else entirely.

#4434. Double guns: ultra-class haul truck packs dual-gun MCS charging, 4 MWh battery

NHL may not be a household name, but its all-new, all-electric NTE240E ultra-class haul track could change that with a 240 ton payload, over 4.1 MWh of battery, advanced regenerative braking, and a world’s first double-gun MCS charging setup.

For the uninitiated, Inner Mongolia North Hauler Joint Stock Co., Ltd. (NHL) is a Chinese heavy equipment manufacturer specializing in the enormous rigid-frame haul trucks used in open-pit mining operations. Established in 1988, NHL has decades of experience building mining trucks for customers around the world, including some of the industry’s largest diesel-electric hybrids. The brand’s new NTE240E is different, representing a company’s real push into battery-electric mining equipment, and it’s powering that push with some seriously ambitious technology.

Let’s start with the battery. The NTE240E packs an absolutely MASSIVE battery pack, with the highest-capacity versions offering up to 4,100 kWh (4.1 MWh) of onboard energy storage. Keeping that much battery topped off is no small task, which is why NHL developed an equally ambitious energy replenishment strategy supporting dual-gun MCS charging, allowing its town-sized battery to go from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

That means operators can take advantage of shift changes and scheduled rest breaks to top off the battery without sacrificing an entire work shift to charging – but even more impressive than the fact that all that juice can be crammed into so big a battery in so little time is the fact that, according to NHL, it can be done at just 25°C (about 77°F).

Plugging in isn’t the only way the NTE240E drinks its juice. NHL’s new dynamic power reception system uses overhead current collectors to supply electricity directly to the truck while it’s climbing loaded mine roads, allowing it to then “ride the brakes” for more energy all the way downhill.

The combined technologies allow NHL’s operators to keep the massive trucks moving without relying entirely on their onboard batteries. The result is a claimed 15% improvement in energy efficiency over the ultra-class industry average.

That efficiency turns into savings, which means the economics of running an NTE240E could be just as compelling as the emissions savings – and those are substantial. NHL says each NTE240E can reduce harmful carbon emissions by more than 2,000 tons annually, even as it cuts operating costs by more than 60% compared to a comparably capable diesel.

What’s more, because the big BEV’s electrical system eliminates the need for engine-related hardware like generators and the maintenance and overhaul costs associated with those components. Taken as a whole, the NHL seems to be a compelling offering … but that’s not for me to say. You guys are the experts – let us know what you think of the new NHL NTE240E, in the comments.

#4433. Gordon Ramsay Is the New Host of the BBC’s ‘Top Gear’

The celebrity chef’s run on the legendary car show is set to start airing in 2028.

At one point, Top Gear was one of the biggest shows on television of any sort. It has been a long time since the glory days of Clarkson, Hammond, and May, though, and multiple efforts to revive the BBC’s legendary automotive series have failed to come close to the impact of the original. The show has not been in production since its newest episodes aired in 2022, but a new host is about to change that very soon. On Wednesday, the BBC announced that celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay is taking over the mantle of Top Gear host starting in 2028. Ramsay will be the first host of the show since production paused after a crash involving then-presenter Freddie Flintoff four years ago.

An announcement from the BBC makes no mention of any potential co-hosts alongside Ramsay, but does add that he will be hosting along with “as yet unnamed co-presenters.” The same announcement quotes BBC Studios Entertainment executive Suzy Lamb as saying that the new Top Gear “won't be a nostalgic reboot" and would instead be a “bold and unmissable new chapter” of the show, lines that suggest a major format change could come with the new host.

While Ramsay is most famous for his career as a chef and host of cooking-related shows, he is also a long-time enthusiast who takes his own cars to the track. He even combined the interests back in 2023, cooking a grilled cheese sandwich in the engine bay of his Aston Martin Valkyrie during a track day. This past weekend, he competed in a celebrity race in Lego Formula 1 cars at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

#4432. Volkswagen’s new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport is the electric hot hatch we want, but can’t have

Volkswagen revealed the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, an electric pocket rocket with a massive rear wing and 362 horsepower.

We knew Volkswagen was cooking something “really spicy” up after teasing the new GTI hot hatch earlier this week.

Volkswagen launched the first-generation Golf GTI in 1976, which essentially defined the hot hatch. To celebrate the brand’s legendary performance badge, a signature of its sporty, practical hatchbacks, VW is entering a new era with its first fully electric GTI.

The GTI has been “one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years,” Volkswagen’s technical development boss, Kai Grünitz, said.

After opening pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, the brand’s first EV to wear the badge, Volkswagen introduced the Clubsport Concept, a souped-up two-door electric pocket rocket.

The new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept shows “how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world,” according to Grünitz.

It’s based on the production ID. Polo GTI uses the same MEB+ platform, but VW reengineered it with a larger electric motor to pump out more power.

The Clubsport is powered by a 362 hp (270 kW) front-mounted electric motor (APP550) that’s typically used in the rear of VW’s larger EVs, like the ID. Tiguan and the ID.7. That’s up considerably from the 233 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft of torque of the standard ID. Polo GTI offers.

Thomas Schmall, CEO of Volkswagen Group Components, said the APP550 motor is “one of the most efficient electric drives in its class.”

Thanks to an electronically controlled front differential lock (VAQ), Volkswagen said, the Clubsport version can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 4.7 seconds, beating the standard ID. Polo GTI by a full two seconds (6.8 seconds).

Volkswagen also fine-tuned the adaptive chassis control (DCC) to make it racetrack-ready and added new ceramic brakes to help slow it down.

The Clubsport version uses the same 52 kW NMC battery as the ID. Polo GTI, which can provide up to 389 hp (290 kW), Volkswagen said, enabling a top speed of 149 mph (240 km/h).

On the exterior, the Clubsport is a two-door model rather than a four-door. It’s 100 mm longer than the standard ID. Polo GTI, with each wing flared an additional 50 mm. It also gets a large motorsport splitter up front, a wider rear end, a new diffuser, and a massive carbon-fiber rear wing.

Inside, the cabin is tailored to the racetrack with a minimalist, stripped-down, two-seater layout. As such, there’s no infotainment system, just a center display to switch between drive modes.

The dash panel, side trims, and other interior elements feature dark ArtVelours microfibre with red topstitching, reinforcing the racetrack-ready interior.

Following the ID. Polo GTI, new ID.3 GTI, and Golf GTI Edition 50, the new ID. Polo Clubsport is the fourth model to debut this year under the performance badge.

Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000). In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the ID.3 GTI, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

And American compact car enthusiasts drool over more unobtanium.

The company will showcase the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport concept car at the Essen Motor Show next week, starting on November 27.

Volkswagen didn’t confirm plans to launch a production version, but don’t expect it to reach the States.

The standard VW ID. Polo and GTI are not sold in the US, so the souped-up Clubsport variant likely won’t be either. Hopefully, VW changes its mind and proves us wrong.

#4428. Carnegie Mellon’s Buggy Is the 100-Year-Old Race Series You Never Knew About, But Won’t Be Able to Stop Watching

Race pits teams against each other to engineer a new vehicle every year that balances aero, handling, and weight, while enabling a driver to somehow squeeze inside.

Ever heard of Buggy? With a capital B? Referring to a specific type of racing? Neither had we, until recently—but where there’s racing, count Road & Track intrigued. Buggy, so you know, is a unique form of racing only taking place at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), and it’s been happening for more than 100 years. Similar to Formula SAE, students engineer, build, and drive the vehicles that compete in the odd spectacle. And yes, in case you were questioning how the buggy is driven, someone is actually inside that tube of carbon fiber.

To understand how this sport works from the car design to the track, Road & Track spoke with Caroline Kiesnowski, the head mechanic and driver for a team. Currently a junior in mechanical engineering at CMU, she broke down what it takes to compete in Buggy.

“Basically, the easiest way to describe it is you put a person in a tube, and you use it as a baton in a relay race,” Kiesnowski says. “You get pushed up two hills, you do a free roll where the driver is completely in control—they're steering and everything—and then you get pushed back up three more hills to a finish line.”

It’s incredibly competitive, with lots of teams vying for the win. Just like professional motorsports, each team designs a new buggy every year using experience from years past and new digital tools to refine the vehicle. The priorities are fairly self explanatory: you want the smallest, lightest buggy possible for being pushed up the hill, then for the downhill sections, designing a buggy with the smallest coefficient of drag and wheels with minimal rolling resistance is paramount. Speeds top out around 40 miles per hour, so these little vehicles are positively cruising at their fastest pace—especially considering their pilots are a foot above the pavement.

The students who end up piloting them are highly recruited, Kiesnowski tells me. Each team wants the smallest possible buggy, which means you need a small person to design the buggy’s body around. If you watch how a driver load into their respective buggy, you’ll quickly understand how tight the squeeze is and how much the design is centered around the driver.

While most of the course is straight or mild curves, there’s one rather challenging turn called The Chute. It’s the source of many crashes and spins, and is something students need to design their buggy around every year. Two layouts are widely used: one is the standard trike that positions two wheels in the rear and one in the front; while the other is the reverse trike, which, logically, puts two wheels up front and one in the rear.

They each have their pros and cons, but in general, the standard trike is thought to be a bit dodgier in The Chute. With only one front wheel controlling steering and turning, it’s a simple design, but ergonomics and visibility for the driver can suffer. Meanwhile, the reverse trikes most often use Ackermann-style steering, which increases complexity, but Kiesnowski finds it to be a better design for steering and braking.

“The steering question is interesting because of the nature of buggy,” Kiesnowski said. “It's in a sense, proprietary information; it's historically been super-secret about people talking about their teams. Some teams even have blacked out windshields, like reflective windshields, so you can't see their steering.”

Another challenge for the track is that said track is actually just a road, and it’s mighty bumpy. Kiesnowski recalls that teams in the past even designed suspension to give the trike a better ride, but it’s a rare design choice that adds weight to a structure you’re trying to keep as light as possible. And yes, there is passing, especially in the downhill roll section, so you could end up doing some proper wheel-to-wheel racing. As you’d expect, though, safety is the number one goal in this whole competition, so drivers have helmets, and there are regulations teams have to follow in building their vehicles to ensure the sport is as safe as possible.

As with any good motorsports event, I asked Kiesnowski about teams trying to bend the rules and regulations for an advantage. She declined to offer details, but still said there have indeed been instances of teams looking for an advantage beyond the book. (After all, the grand prize of pride and bragging rights over your peers is a mighty tempting trophy in college.)

The competition takes place every April at Carnegie Mellon’s campus in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And while the engines are essentially members of the team pushing, it’s still a form of racing we can get excited about.

#4427. Tesla FSD approved in Italy, the first big EU market to say yes

Italy’s transport ministry has granted provisional approval to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” in Europe. Italy becomes the 12th European country to allow the system, and the first of the EU’s big markets.

It also didn’t wait for Brussels. The EU committee that decides on bloc-wide recognition isn’t expected to vote until December at the earliest.

Deputy Prime Minister and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini announced the decision on X on Friday. He wrote that the ministry (MIT) gave the green light after a “thorough technical feasibility check,” and that Italy is getting ahead of the EU recognition process, which he described as “still being defined.”

Tesla Europe followed with a one-liner, “Now approved in Italy, rollout begins soon,” and a video of one of its cars driving itself through Rome. There’s no firm rollout date yet.

It’s still a Level 2 driver-assist system. It can steer, brake, accelerate, and handle intersections and lane changes, but the driver has to supervise at all times and stays fully responsible for the car.

The Dutch vehicle authority RDW was first, approving FSD Supervised on April 10 under Article 39 of the EU type-approval regulation. Other member states can then recognize that approval nationally, one by one.

Ten did before Italy: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Those are mostly small markets. Together with the Netherlands, they add up to about 70 million people, or roughly 15% of the EU’s population.

Italy alone has about 59 million people, so Friday’s decision nearly doubles the share of Europeans who can legally use the system, to close to 30%.

Rome’s position moved fast. In April, Senator Carlo Calenda formally asked Salvini’s ministry to prioritize the approval. On October 29, Salvini posted that he’d had a “very positive and constructive” call with Elon Musk and that Italy supported a “swift EU approval,” which read at the time as backing for an EU-level decision, not a national one. Three weeks later, Italy went national.

A lot changed in between. Tesla dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe after Germany’s Transport Ministry called it misleading, and cut the maximum speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit. Then on November 16, the RDW approved stricter driver monitoring, including hands on the wheel above 130 km/h. That’s the version Italy is approving.

The EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) pushed the Tesla vote to December after holding only discussions in October. Bloc-wide approval needs a qualified majority: at least 15 of 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Germany said in October it would back approval after Tesla agreed to the rename and the speed cap. If it follows through, Germany and the 12 approving countries would cover roughly 47% of the EU’s population.

That’s progress for Tesla, but it’s not 65%. France refused a national approval in July, and Spain hasn’t recognized the Dutch approval. Tesla needs at least one of them, plus most of the remaining holdouts.

I used FSD for five days this past week. It's impressive on controlled roads.

Even in Chill driving mode, there were still more than a few times that I had to use the Critical feedback.

To think it will ever be perfect is pure fantasy. I will never climb into a automobile that does not have steering controls.

Seven repairs and $10,000 on a leaky roof in two years, with no guarantees. When you factor in Musk, I'm done.

Both Carmax and OnlyUsedTesla acknowledged receiving my requests. No offers from either service 48-hours later. Guess I'm not the only one that's done with Tesla.

This is a real win for Tesla, and for Italian owners with HW4 cars who have been paying for a feature they couldn’t use at home. Italy is Tesla’s first big European market to say yes, and it shifts momentum going into December.

But it’s pretty crazy that now Europe is going to get a safer FSD than in the US.

I bet that this will get reflected in the data, if we ever get to see it.

#4426. An Empty EV Tried To Park Itself 868 Times In One Night. The Video Is Hilarious

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Correcting yourself while parking isn't an abnormal event. Maybe you overshot the turn and pulled just a little bit too close to the car next to you. So you back out, adjust, and try again. It's not all that embarrassing—at least not the first time. But how many times does it have to happen before you start to go red in the face (or just give up and drive away)?

Two? Five? What about 868? Because that's how many times one Chinese EV was caught on security camera footage trying to find the perfect parking spot overnight.

An apparently empty Avatr EV was caught on camera spending the majority of the night maneuvering around marked parking spaces in a parking structure in China's Anhui Province. The car can be seen on video moving around a small area of the garage. Reversing into a space, pulling forward, repositioning, and doing it all over again.

Watching the footage is a bit confusing. If you know that it's a car with parking assist or other autonomy features, you probably assume that the car is just having trouble deciding how well it's parked—like it's some sort of programming error that makes the car's software lack confidence that its parking job is good enough. That may not have been the case here.

It turns out that this particular car wasn't alone in its parking shenanigans. In fact, other video footage soon emerged showing other Avatr and Huajing-branded cars pulling off similar parking stunts.

While the exact reasoning for the repeated parking is unknown, CarNewsChina quickly put together that the cars in the videos all sport Huawei's driver assistance software.

The footage emerged just as a contest run by Huawei was taking place. It ran through November 13th and was meant to show off the capabilities of the tech company's Qiankun Intelligent Driving system by giving users points in eight different categories depending on how they used vehicles' Qiankun-backed features while driving.

One of these categories is called "Parking Elite." It measures the use of Automatic Parking Assist, Exit-and-Park Assist, Parking Lot Navigation Assist, and Remote Parking Assist to assign points to drivers. The top 100 drivers would receive Huawei points, which can be redeemed for in-app purchases and discounts.

Of course, this reportedly led to some drivers attempting to game the system. CarNewsChina even surfaces a post where one driver claims to have completed 1,000 parking sessions in a single day. It's worth noting that Huawei's tech is technically a driver-assistance feature and not an autonomous driving function; the car is supposed to always have a human supervising these types of actions

These are just theories, of course, but the claims from drivers and security camera footage do seem like gaming the system is a plausible explanation.

Either way, you have to admit that if you saw a car parking itself 868 times overnight into various parking spaces, you'd wonder what was going on—I know I would. At least it's good for a laugh and didn't cause a traffic jam.

#4425. Renault undercuts BYD with a new EV that costs less than $20,000

The new Renault Twingo E-Tech is among the most affordable vehicles, electric or gas-powered, starting at just £14,745 in the UK, or under $20,000.

Another affordable, practical EV the US will never see. Renault’s new Twingo E-Tech is an electric remake of its iconic 1990s city car.

The retro-looking EV went on sale in Europe earlier this year, starting at under €20,000 ($22,000), before government incentives. In places like Germany, it starts at about €13,990 ($15,500), including the €6,000 ($6,600) federal EV grant.

In the UK, Renault announced that prices for the Twingo E-Tech will start at just £14,745, or about $19,500. That includes the government’s Electric Clean Car Grant (ECG) of £3,750 ($4,900).

At that price, Renault’s new electric car is among the most affordable vehicles available, including gas-powered cars.

It’s cheaper than the gas-powered Dacia Sandero (£14,765) and BYD’s cheapest EV, the Dolphin Surf (£18,675). Only a few cars are lower-priced, including the Dacia Spring (£11,990) and Leapmotor T03 (£12,995).

What do you get for the price? At just 3,790 mm (149.2″) long, the electric city car is a bit smaller than the Hyundai Inster and the BYD Dolphin Surf.

For those in the US, that’s even smaller than the first-generation Chevy Bolt EV, which measured 4,145 mm (163.2″) in length.

Despite its compact size, the “cheeky, practical” 5-door city car, as Renault calls it, offers up to 360 liters of boot capacity. It also features independent, sliding 50/50 folding rear seats to haul bigger items like a surfboard.

With up to 50 kW DC fast charging, Renault said the Twingo E-Tech can charge from 15% to 80% in 28 minutes.

The base Renault Twingo E-Tech Evolution, priced from £14,745 ($19,500), uses a 27.5 kWh LFP battery and an 80 hp (60 kW) motor, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range.

The entry-level version features 16″ steel wheels, a 7″ driver display, 10″ navigation screen, and ADAS features, including cruise control and lane-keep assist.

Renault will offer three Twingo E-Tech trims in total. The mid-range Techno trim gains 18″ wheels, Google built-in with Renault’s Reno avatar, a reversing camera, automatic climate control, a hands-free key card, One Pedal driving, and heated front seats. It starts at £16,245 ($21,500), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG.

With Google built in, drivers can easily find and navigate to charging stations via Google Maps, use Google Gemini AI virtual assistance, or access over 100 apps, including Waze and Amazon Music.

At least this car has some styling unlike the generic box style VW offerings in this category. In this size car I prefer the SUV style of the Dacia Spring for myself, but of course we will never see any of these wonderful cars in the USA.

The top-spec Twingo E-Tech Launch Edition, priced from £17,645 ($23,200), including the £3,750 ($4,900) ECG, adds a suite of ADAS features, including blind-spot warning, rear cross-traffic alert and hands-free parking.

Inside, the Launch Edition features a special mottled textile upholstery with red stitching and premium floor mats.

Renault is offering a special promo for those who buy a new Twingo E-Tech through Mobilize Financial Services on a PCP or HP agreement by June 30, 2027, which includes two years’ free servicing.

Interested buyers can purchase the Twingo R Pass for £100, giving them priority access to ordering, a mini Twingo E-Tech model, and a green Renault key cover.

It marks the first time an Acura-badged car has officially been sold in Japan.

While it may be the luxury offshoot of Honda, Acura’s cars have never actually been sold in Japan in any official capacity. The luxury automaker has been focused on North America for almost the entirety of its four decades of existence, meaning that any Acura cars in the brand’s would-be home country are either imported or modified cars initially sold as Hondas.

That finally changes today. As of Wednesday, the Acura Integra Type S is now on sale in Japan, fulfilling a promise made earlier this year. In addition to being the first Acura to reach that market, it is the first variant of the new Integra to be sold outside of North America in any form.

Acura has been teasing the possibility of the Integra Type S reaching the Japanese market all year, starting with a production model conspicuously on display among Honda’s Tokyo Auto Salon offerings in January. The Integra was shown again at another Japanese show in February before production plans were confirmed in March. Now, Japanese buyers will actually be able to get their hands on the Ohio-built Integra.

The Acura shares an engine and many other parts with the Honda Civic Type R, but the pair diverge in a few key ways. While the Integra is softer and more refined, the Honda is sharper and more harsh. American buyers could pick freely between the two, but other markets have not had the option to do so until now. It’s good news for Japanese enthusiasts looking for a slightly different flavor of performance Honda—a list that includes noted Integra Type S fan Yuki Tsunoda.

This kei truck is currently up for auction on Bring a Trailer.

Toyota’s surprising decision to start selling new kei trucks under the Scion brand in the United States as low-speed vehicles (LSVs) has generated a lot of excitement. How could it now? Just look how cute these little trucks are. It’s enough to make you want to drive to Costco and bring home a single large box of cereal tied down in the pint-sized bed.

But why wait for the Scion to get here? Right now, there’s a legally imported keijidosha pickup over at Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos): a 2000 Daihatsu HiJet, which happens to be the same model on which the new Scion is based.

Even if these wee haulers look like they've escaped from the pages of a Richard Scarry book, the kei truck segment is serious business in Japan. Over there, these little pickups work just as hard as larger trucks, carrying a little less cargo but doing the work of road repair, smaller construction projects, plumbing work, and, of course, gardening. For the latter, there's even an annual competition to put together the best bonsai garden in a kei truck bed.

See all results for used cars for sale near 97058

On this side of the Pacific, you'll need to carefully check what your state laws say about the use of kei trucks on public roads, as some states allow them to be driven on roads with a speed limit of 35 mph or less, while others only allow them to be used on private property.

Even with those restrictions, this HiJet would be incredibly useful for ferrying around livestock feed on a farm, or shuttling small deliveries around a busy factory complex, or even getting evil minions around a hollowed-out volcano lair. If it does pass muster for on-road use where you live, these trucks are surprisingly plucky to drive, and would make for the ultimate DIY partner. Plenty of hunters and fishermen also appreciate four-wheel-drive kei trucks for their ability to squeeze down narrow tracks where full-size pickups can't go.

The bed is also surprisingly flexible, with fold-down sides that transform it into a mini-flatbed truck. The payload is stouter than you'd think, rated for 770 pounds, so though it may be tiny, it's still mighty.

Daihatsu has plenty of experience building kei trucks and cars, including as a subcontractor for other companies, including Toyota. The HiJet has been around since the 1960s, making it Japan's version of the F-150.

Motive power comes from a 659cc three-cylinder engine plonked in the middle of the chassis, good for a whopping 42 horsepower. That power goes to the rear wheels through a five-speed manual transmission, or you can hit a button and get power to all four corners. The selling dealer has recently replaced the battery and done a mild tune-up, including new spark plugs and an oil change.
